title: ACMap: Across-scales Connectivity Mapping of Primate Brain
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper tackles the challenging problem of reconstructing brain-wide structural connectivity from virus tracing data and linking it to dMRI-based tractography. Bridging connectivity across spatial scales is a key open problem in computational neuroscience. The authors formulate streamline reconstruction from tracer intensity as a continuous front propagation problem governed by the Eikonal equation and solved using FMM. This is an interpretable alternative to traditional neuron tracing methods that often rely on discrete skeletonization or heuristic graph-based approaches. More importantly, the proposed methods are claimed to operate fast at the scale of the whole brain, which is an important strength. Compared to existing neuron tracing methods (e. g. , NeuTube, APP2, Rivulet2), the method appears to better capture dense fiber bundles, which is important for mesoscale connectivity analysis.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: A central concern is that there is no true ground-truth for the reported streamline reconstruction, yet the evaluation relies heavily on comparing reconstructed streamlines to the raw tracer intensity. Virus tracing data are known to be noisy and contain artifacts (e. g. , vasculature signal, non-specific labeling), which may not correspond to true axonal pathways. This directly affects: ○ The speed function assumption (intensity → axon likelihood), which may not hold in practice. ○ The Dice, which are computed against raw intensity and therefore may not reflect biologically meaningful accuracy. Additionally, the Dice score is computed on binarized maps, but the paper does not specify how the threshold is selected or how sensitive the results are to this choice. Since thresholding can significantly affect Dice scores of different methods, this raises concerns about reproducibility and the fairness of comparison. The method assumes that higher tracer intensity corresponds to higher axon likelihood and thus faster propagation. However, given noise, artifacts, and variability in tracer uptake, this assumption may not be robust and could lead to biased or spurious pathways. The paper lacks validation of whether reconstructed streamlines correspond to known anatomical targets. For example, the authors could validate whether distal projection regions match established connectivity patterns reported in prior tracing or connectivity studies. In the current format, it is unclear whether the method reconstructs biologically meaningful pathways or simply follows noisy intensity patterns. There is no clear visualization of: ○ Whole-brain reconstructed fibers ○ Regional streamlines overlaid on raw tracer intensity ○ Direct comparison overlays between ACMap, baseline methods, and dMRI Such visualizations are critical for assessing the fidelity and anatomical plausibility of the results.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The topic of this submission is within the scope of this conference. The text is straightforward to understand for a reader with knowledge in recent approaches for image analysis. The work described here is interesting and provides a demonstrated and considerable advance over previous approaches.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: A minor issue: Apparently, the letter \mu is missing in several locations, which led to some confusion. It is also suggested to use either italic or regular letters for units consistently.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The ACMap method achieves excellent tractography reconstruction performance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Evaluations on more diverse datasets are still lacking. Additional tests across multiple independent datasets would further verify the strong robustness of this method and enhance its credibility.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We summarized the main critiques into 5 categories and provided responses with Rx-y referring to the response to comment #y from reviewer #x. Category 1: Lack of biological ground-truth and unvalidated assumption R1-1 and R1-3: We respectfully note that, despite the fact that no method is an “absolute” gold standard for tracing axonal pathways, among all the tracing techniques, virus tracing is widely regarded as one of the closest experimental proxies for axonal connectivity (e.g. Refs 1,12). It has also been uniformly considered as gold standard for the diffusion-MRI-based tractography method evaluation (e.g. Refs. 1, 8,10, 12). Beyond MR field, the more general basic neuroscientific field endorses the validity of virus tracing, as demonstrated by Allen Brain Atlas mouse connectome (Wang et al., Cell 2020; PMID: 32386544). The virus-tracing dataset adopted in this study had already undergone rigorous artifact mitigation by the original providers (Ref. 17), with this artifact-removal procedure further enhanced by multiple steps in ACMap. Category 2: Evaluation and robustness R1-1 and R1-2: We followed a widely used evaluation method of setting a voxel to 1 if traversed by at least one streamline and 0 otherwise (e.g. Wakana et al., Neuroimage 2007; PMID: 17481925) for Dice score evaluation, and applied this evaluation to ACMap and all competing methods. We also reported AUC (Fig. 5), a threshold-independent metric (Ref. 12). We will clarify the evaluation above in the revised manuscript. Category 3: Validation and visualization R1-4: The reconstructed commissural and projection fibers align with the pathways well characterized and delineated in a histology-based marmoset atlas book (Paxinos et al., 2025). Specifically, commissural fibers matched canonical interhemispheric tracts; and projection fibers followed atlas-defined trajectories from cortex through the internal capsule and cerebral peduncle. Paxinos, G., et al. (2025). The marmoset brain in stereotaxic coordinates. Academic press. R1-5 and R1-8: For clearer visualization, we will generate a figure including enlarged streamlines overlaid on raw virus-tracer intensity maps for ACMap and all competing methods included in the paper in GitHub repository. Understanding the limitation of limited injection site of adopted marmoset virus tracing dataset, we will also extensively and rigorously validate ACMap using Allen Institute mouse virus-tracing data with thousands of injection sites (Ref. Wang et al., Cell 2020). R1-7: The injection site was already delineated by the original dataset providers (Ref. 17) using a rigorous method to localize and detect labeled cell bodies with intensity above a certain threshold as the injection site. Despite robustness of injection site localization for virus tracing, we agree for validation of other fiber tracing method, precise registration of injection site (translated to fiber tractography initialization location) is critical and will be discussed in the revised manuscript. Category 4: Computational eﬃciency R1-9: We respectfully clarify a possible misreading: the manuscript does not claim computational speed as a contribution. “Fast Marching Method” is the standard name of a well-established algorithm (Ref. 15), not a statement about ACMap’s runtime performance. We will add a runtime analysis and discuss that GPU acceleration could substantially improve ACMap’s efficiency in the revised manuscript. Category 5: Minor concerns R1-6 and R1-8: In Fig. 6a, the dMRI streamlines appear to exit the brain due to a surface-rendering artifact. In the original 3D volume, the streamlines remain within the brain mask, and tractography was performed following Ref. 22.R2-1: We will restore the missing µ symbols and harmonize the units throughout the manuscript. R4-1: We agree that evaluation across multiple datasets would further strengthen the study. We will note this for future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Two reviewers support acceptance and acknowledge the methodological novelty and the meaningful cross-scale value of ACMap’s brain connectivity research, whereas one reviewer raises substantial critical limitations. To resolve the conflicting reviews, the authors must fully address the key critical points raised by Reviewer 1, including the lack of biological ground truth, unreliable evaluation based on noisy virus tracing signals, unclear threshold setting for Dice metrics, unvalidated assumption between tracer intensity and axon likelihood, ambiguous injection site localization, insufficient anatomical validation and comprehensive visualizations, as well as missing computational efficiency analysis. Minor concerns, such as limited dataset diversity, formal notation inconsistencies and problematic dMRI preprocessing artifacts, should also be addressed concisely in the rebuttal. | After reviewing the initial feedback, the author’s rebuttal, and the post-rebuttal comments, I recommend rejecting this paper for several reasons. The main issue is the lack of independent biological ground truth for the streamline reconstruction task. The evaluation relies solely on comparing reconstructed streamlines with the raw tracer data used to generate them, creating a circular validation. Although virus tracing offers insights into brain connectivity, it has significant noise and artifacts that can lead to misleading reconstructions. The authors claim that higher tracer intensity indicates a higher likelihood of axons, but they provide no evidence to support this assumption. Furthermore, they assert that reconstructed fibers align with known pathways in the Paxinos marmoset brain atlas but provide no corroborating evidence, such as visualizations or quantitative comparisons. The promise of improved visualizations post-acceptance does not compensate for the lack of validation in the manuscript. The authors also fail to clarify how the threshold for Dice score calculations was chosen, affecting the reliability of their comparative evaluations. Additionally, key methodological details, such as the injection site localization and computational efficiency analysis, remain unclear. The rebuttal focuses on commitments for future improvements rather than evidence from the submitted manuscript. Acceptance should be based solely on the current submission, not on promises of additional work. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I think the authors did a good job addressing the concerns of Rev. 1 in the rebuttal. Unfortunately, ground truths are not available for tractography. The authors proposed a robust method for predicting streamlines from virus-tracing data, which is a step forward in developing silver standards for assessing tractography methods. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers recommended acceptance. The authors have adequately addressed the reviewers’ questions and concerns. The paper is therefore recommended for acceptance.

title: ALSAnchorNet: Biologically Informed Multimodal MRI Fusion for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed modules for ALS classification are logical ones to solve the given problem. The major module is based on biological knowledge of frontal lobe vulnerability. In addition, the study will contribute to addressing the scarcity of ALS imaging datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: They use clinical variables including PVS, etc. (dim = 93). Details are needed on the meaning and size of the variables. Why do you use a common MLP for FC and SC? Since these are two different modalities, modality-specific encoders make more sense. There should be an ablation study on this. Five-fold cross-validation might cause bias. Since the ALS/CN ratio is imbalanced, they should apply a stratified cross-validation maintaining the ratio of the two classes. Tables 1 and 2 lack p-values comparing their method with other baselines. This is a single-center study lacking external validation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The study is evaluated on one of the largest ALS cohorts reported to date. 2.The model architecture and input design are informed by prior biological knowledge, using a cross-attention mechanism to encode frontal lobe vulnerability. 3.The framework incorporates multimodal biomarkers, which help improve diagnostic performance and provide complementary information beyond connectivity features.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Baselines appear to be collapsing to the majority class since the recall is 1 for FC + SC only and MLP fusion. 2.Weak baseline models. Classic connectome-specific baselines, such as BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN, Brain Network Transformer, etc., are not chosen. 3.No variance reporting. Only mean 5-fold CV metrics are reported, standard deviations are not reported in tables 1 and 2. 4.Figure 1 inconsistency. FC and SC dimensions are visually different, while the text mentioned they are the same dimension. 5.Poor methodological clarity. The paper states that d_c = 60,516 is the vectorized upper-triangular dimension of a 246*246 matrix, which is contradictory. In the Method section, the text “partition the connectivity embeddings” is misleading since the h_p and h_p,; appear to be created using different MLPs. Eq 3 and Eq 4 define K and V with dimensions d_k and d_v, which is inaccurate since K and V need to be the same dimension The implementation details describe a two-layer classifier (128 -> 64 -> 2), but Eq 10 only shows a single linear layer, which is contradictory 6.One of the claimed contributions, the Fusion Refinement Encoder, appears to be simply a concatenation operation followed by an MLP, which does not seem sufficiently novel.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed FAA explicitly encodes known ALS vulnerability, making the model more meaningful than conventional DL fusion. Their design combines connectivity with glymphatic and CSF biomarkers, demonstrating clear complementary gains beyond FC or SC alone. Their approach shows increasing clinical credibility since region-level and connectivity analyses align with known motor network pathology.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The methodological contribution in this work seems incremental rather than fundamentally something new. The proposed “anchor attention” is a simple adaptation of standard attention with a predefined region. Additionally, fixing the frontal lobe as the anchor is not learned or validated and this may bias the proposed model and limit generalization to other ALS patterns. In current work the fusion is largely MLP-based with simple concatenation and refinement. No strong comparison to more advanced cross-modal methods was reported which is very important. The performed evaluation is limited to a relatively small cohort, with only moderate performance (accuracy: 77%), and without any external validation. It is unclear how well the proposed model generalizes.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing our contributions: the biologically grounded design (all reviewers), one of the largest single-center ALS multimodal MRI cohort to date (R2), and the clinical credibility of our findings (R4). We address the main concerns below. 1.Methodological Clarifications (Meta, R2) (1) d_c dimension (R2): We apologize for the typo. We use the full FC/SC matrix as input. We will remove the word “upper-triangular”. (2) Modality-specific encoders (R1-Q2, R2): h_p (FC) and h_{p} (SC) are produced by separate, modality-specific MLPs, not a shared encoder. We use different colors of MLP blocks in Figure 1 to indicate this, but provided the incorrect description in the Method section. We will rewrite the corresponding method section as “modality-specific embedding via two parallel MLPs.” and update equation (1) to reflect this. (3) Eq. 3–4 (R2): We fully agree K and V matrix should share the same sequence length. We incorrectly use the same symbol for both the dimension of the K matrix and the normalization scale factor d_k, We will revise the method description to clarify. (4) Eq. 10 (R2): Equation (10) will be corrected to reflect the two-layer classifier (128→64→2) used in implementation. (5) Figure 1 (R2): FC and SC are indeed the same dimension; the visual difference was an illustration artifact and will be corrected. (6) Clinical variables (R1-Q1): The 93-dim vector comprises 3 ChP, 3 gBOLD, 70 FWF, 11 ALPS, and 6 PVS features. We will add this in Section 2. 2.Statistical Rigor (Meta, R1, R2) Our 5-fold CV was stratified by class (R1-Q3); we will state this explicitly. Standard deviations across folds and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against each baseline will be added to Tables 1 and 2 in the camera-ready version. 3.Baselines (R2, R4) Recall = 1.0 on weaker baselines (R2-Q1): This reflects collapse to the majority class (ALS), which actually highlights the difficulty of the task and the value of our biologically informed design — ALSAnchorNet avoids this collapse and achieves balanced sensitivity and specificity. Connectome-specific baselines (R2-Q2, R4): We have compared SOTA methods in the ALS diagnosis task. Since the original papers did not provide specific names for their methodologies, we refer to them as CNN, GNN, and Transformer in the manuscript. Furthermore, the selected baselines include established CNN/GNN/Transformer-based frameworks, which represent the core innovations of BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN, and Brain Network Transformer, respectively. In contrast, our approach selects similar methodologies that are more specifically designed for ALS. To clarify that we have compared SOTA methods, we will update the naming of the baseline methods to ‘XXX et al.’ in the revised manuscript and include broader comparisons in the journal extension. 4.Novelty and Design (R4, R2-Q6) We acknowledge that our contribution lies more in designing an appropriate method for an important and underexplored clinical application than in proposing fundamentally new machinery. To our knowledge, this is the first framework integrating connectomics with glymphatic/CSF biomarkers for ALS, and the first to encode frontal-lobe vulnerability as an architectural prior. FAA is not generic attention — its query is anatomically constrained to the frontal subnetwork, which is precisely what lets the biological prior shape whole-brain interactions. Fixing the anchor (R4) is intentional; learning it would discard the prior knowledge motivating the design. 5.Generalization (R1-Q5, R4) We acknowledge the single-center limitation. Multimodal MRI ALS datasets are extremely scarce, which motivates our public data release of the processed data (159 ALS/107 HC). Cross-site validation will be reported in future work. We will incorporate all clarifications and corrections in the camera-ready version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents ALSAnchorNet, which combines an attention network for intra- and inter-frontal structural/functional connectivities with glymphatic and CSF biomarker features, to identify ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis). The paper lacks statistical evaluation and comparison with advanced architectures, as all reviewers consistently pointed out. Although conducting more experiments is not asked during the rebuttal phase, they should be clarified in the rebuttal. The clarification questions about the methodology part need to be answered in the rebuttal. | The rebuttal sufficiently addressed reviewers’ questions regarding the clarification of the methodology and details of the experiments. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend accept: post-rebuttal R1 and R2 both raised to Accept and the rebuttal addressed the primary AC’s methodology clarifications. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper’s main contribution is a biologically informed multimodal ALS diagnosis framework that combines connectivity features with glymphatic and CSF biomarkers, together with a clinically meaningful dataset that reviewers viewed as valuable to the field. The rebuttal did not eliminate every concern, yet it appears to have satisfactorily clarified several technical points and preserved positive reviewer support after rebuttal. On balance, the paper’s contribution to ALS imaging analysis and multimodal modeling is sufficient to justify acceptance despite some methodological limitations.

title: BrainKODE: Controlled Koopman Dynamics over Longitudinal Structure–Function Coupling for Early Prediction of Adolescent Substance Use
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.There are three core innovations in this manuscript which are all coherently motivated and cleanly composed. Riemannian longitudinal alignment, adaptive cross-modal coupling gates, and semigroup-constrained Koopman evolution. Additionally, to enforce SPD structure on SC via diffusion operators so both modalities share the same Riemannian treatment is particularly elegant. 2.The +10.4 pp sensitivity gain over the closest Koopman baseline (NeuroKoop) and the notably balanced sensitivity/specificity (85.18/85.78%) are clinically meaningful results for an imbalanced dataset (∼23% positive rate). Most competing methods sacrifice sensitivity badly under this imbalance. 3.Table 2 systematically decomposes contributions across geometry, coupling, dynamics, and context, with four well-defined research questions. The finding that removing Riemannian alignment drops accuracy by ~9 pp is compelling and convincingly justifies the geometric machinery.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The cohort-level Fréchet mean G is computed across “all training subjects and visits. “ It is critical to clarify whether this anchor is recomputed strictly within each cross-validation fold’s training split, or computed once across the full dataset. 2.The dataset is substantially imbalanced (579 SUI vs. 1,908 non-SUI, roughly 1:3.3). The paper only reports accuracy and sensitivity/specificity alone; AUROC and balanced accuracy should also be reported here. 3.The experiments are conducted on a relatively small parcellation of 53 networks, yet no analysis of computational cost, memory usage, or scalability to finer parcellations (e. g. , N=200+) is provided. This is a notable practical gap, as many fMRI related applications require higher-resolution connectomes. 3.(Minor) Reference 1 and 2 are duplicated.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper’s major strength is its well-integrated formulation of longitudinal brain risk prediction. Rather than treating structural and functional connectivity as static or independently fused inputs, it models their evolving coupling across development, which is better aligned with the neurodevelopmental nature of adolescent substance use risk. A second strength is the geometry-aware design: mapping connectomes into a shared Riemannian space is an interesting way to improve cross-visit consistency. The semigroup-constrained Koopman formulation is also appealing because it imposes temporally coherent multi-step evolution from baseline.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper’s mechanistic claims are stronger than its evidence. Although BrainKODE is framed as learning developmental structure–function dynamics, the experiments mainly show improved prediction, not that the learned coupling gates truly reflect neurobiological coupling mechanisms. The contextual module is also only weakly validated, since gradient-based importance does not demonstrate how context changes latent trajectories. In addition, the evaluation relies on 5-fold cross-validation only, without more stringent tests of site, scanner, or demographic robustness that would strengthen the clinical claim.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important problem: modeling longitudinal brain development instead of using static connectivity. This is well motivated. 2.The experiments include comparisons and ablation, and the performance looks better than baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The method assumes that brain development can be modeled as a linear dynamical system in latent space. This is a strong assumption, but the paper does not provide enough discussion or validation to support it. 2.The results are reported as mean ± std, but no statistical testing is provided to support the performance gains. 3.Evaluation is limited to one dataset. All experiments are conducted on the ABCD dataset. It is unclear whether the method generalizes to other datasets or populations.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for their feedback. We first address the AC’s central concern, followed by reviewer-specific responses. Validation beyond predictive accuracy [AC, R2, R4]: BrainKODE validates learned developmental dynamics through three complementary mechanisms beyond outcome prediction. (i) Trajectory reconstruction. The controlled evolution h_hat_{t+Delta} = U(Delta) h_hat_t + B c_tilde_t (Eq. 2), initialized at h_0, is constrained by L_dyn (Eq. 3) to reconstruct observed intermediate embeddings h_2 and h_4, providing label-independent validation of longitudinal trajectories. (ii) Structural constraints. U(Delta)=exp(Delta Omega) enforces the semigroup property U(Delta_1+Delta_2)=U(Delta_1)U(Delta_2), ensuring temporally consistent evolution under a shared operator. Removing Koopman dynamics or the semigroup constraint degrades performance (Tab. 2; 77.42% and 82.50% vs. 85.64%), indicating reliance on consistent dynamics rather than static representations. (iii) Biological coherence. Learned coupling patterns (Fig. 2) show systematic longitudinal differences, including strengthened CON–SMN/VSN interactions and reduced DMN integration in SUI, consistent with prior neurodevelopmental findings. Fréchet mean / metrics / scalability / refs [R1]: The Fréchet anchor G is recomputed within each cross-validation training fold only, preventing test-data leakage. Despite class imbalance, BrainKODE achieves balanced sensitivity/specificity (85.18%/85.78%) with 85.64% balanced accuracy, exceeding all baselines in Tab.1.Computationally, the framework remains tractable through sparse multiplex graphs (k=7), a single GAT layer, and Koopman evolution on pooled visit embeddings rather than full graph tensors. Ref. [1] and [2] will be merged. Mechanistic vs predictive [R2.1]: BrainKODE’s mechanistic claims rest on L_dyn enforced trajectory reconstruction and systematic time-evolving coupling, not on causal attribution. The γ-ablation reduces accuracy from 85.64% to 81.37% (Tab. 2), indicating that adaptive coupling is functionally necessary. Coupling patterns also evolve systematically across visits (Fig. 2), supporting that γ captures organized developmental structure. Context enters dynamics through B c_tilde_t (Eq. 2), directly modulating latent evolution within the controlled dynamical formulation. Robustness and generalization [R2.2 / R4.3]: ABCD is a large-scale multi-site cohort spanning 21 sites and multiple scanner platforms; subject-level stratified cross-validation evaluates generalization across this heterogeneity. Moreover, we performed leave-one-site-out evaluation across multiple major ABCD sites (holding out each site entirely for testing and averaging performance across held-out sites), achieving 83.22% ± 0.11 accuracy, 82.73% ± 0.24 sensitivity, and 83.36% ± 0.10 specificity, supporting robust cross-site generalization. Linearity assumption [R4.1]: Koopman theory states that nonlinear systems admit linear representations in sufficiently rich observable spaces. In BrainKODE, the geometry-aware multiplex encoder defines this latent space, while U(Delta) governs the resulting latent evolution. Thus, linearity enables stable and temporally consistent dynamics rather than imposing a restrictive assumption. Removing Koopman dynamics reduces accuracy to 77.42% (Tab. 2). Statistical testing [R4.2]: Paired t-tests across the 5 CV folds against the strongest baseline NeuroKoop yielded significant improvements with p=0.016 (accuracy), p=0.006 (sensitivity), and p=0.040 (specificity). One-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests further yielded p=0.0312 for accuracy and sensitivity, as BrainKODE outperformed NeuroKoop on every fold; specificity showed consistent directional improvement (p=0.063; 85.78% vs. 84.91%). Tab. 2 further shows systematic degradation across ablations, confirming that gains arise from structured modeling.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): As acknowledged by the reviewers, the proposed framework is very novel. The one concern that I’d hope the authors to respond to is whether there are ways to validate the value of the method beyond predictive accuracy, given the focus on learning multi-modal developmental dynamics. | The manuscript receives mixed rating post rebuttal. After careful consideration, my assessment is that the weaknesses outweigh the strengths. The proposal is novel, but arguably extremely complex. To this end, the experiments failed to justify the need for the over-engineering over existing SC-FC methods. In particular, only one of the baselines is a SC-FC coupling method (others are generic GNN methods) despite that there are many papers on SC-FC coupling in past MICCAIs alone, e.g., DFSC,HKC, joint GCN. Moreover, the rebuttal did not successfully address the interpretability problem, which is a critical concern for this overly complex method. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I think that the idea is interesting. Although some weaknesses still remain, I thought that authors have provided a good discussion on this early-stage but interesting research, and have provided some convincing responses to specific critiques. I strongly encourage authors to include better clarifications and revisions as suggested by reviewers to strengthen the final version. I would argue for accept. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews are inclined towards acceptance. R4 still questions generality of the method, but given limited nature with datasets in medical imaging and that CV has been used for evaluation, I would recommend accepting the paper.

title: Bridging Single Distortion Artifacts and Multifactorial Clinical Quality: Few-Shot Biparametric MRI Quality Assessment via Distortion-Trained Prototypical Networks
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clinically important and well-motivated problem of prostate MRI quality assessment under the PI-QUAL standard, with a focus on real-world challenges such as class imbalance and the scarcity of diverse low-quality samples. 2.The two-stage learning strategy is practical, leveraging comparatively objective distortion labels to facilitate learning for a more complex and clinically relevant task, with potential to generalize to other medical imaging scenarios.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.While the paper is motivated by data scarcity, the experimental dataset (Dataset 1) contains 1027 samples, which does not represent a strictly low-data regime. The results in Table 1 show that a standard fully supervised baseline (FSL), trained on the full training split, already achieves strong performance and outperforms the proposed method. This raises the concern that the few-shot formulation may not provide practical benefits in this scenario and appears somewhat driven by methodology rather than data constraints. 2.A more realistic evaluation protocol is needed, where instead of constructing episodic tasks on the test set, the meta-trained model should also be evaluated under a direct inference setting by being applied to the test data without forming support/query splits. This setting is more consistent with real-world deployment and aligns with recent trends in few-shot learning, where non-episodic evaluation has become increasingly common. 3.It is important to report the performance of a fully supervised model on the PRIME dataset (FSL baseline). Regardless of whether the results are strong or not, including this baseline would provide a clearer comparison of the benefits of the proposed approach.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper develops a few-shot framework tailored for prostate MRI quality assessment, effectively addressing the scarcity of clinically annotated data. 2.It leverages structural T2WI as an anatomical reference to help distinguish true anatomical variation from geometric distortion in DWI. 3.It introduces feature alignment modules (FiLM and GRL) to improve robustness to variations in scanning parameters.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper is presented as prostate MRI quality assessment, but the method is mainly built around distortion representation learning and is clinically validated only on binary PI-QUAL classification. 2.The method is sensitive to support-set selection, which may affect robustness in few-shot adaptation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem. MRI quality assessment, especially for DWI, is important in prostate imaging and has clear practical value. 2.The overall motivation is sensible. Using a more objective and easier-to-label distortion task as a source task for transfer to a more subjective and data-scarce clinical quality task is an interesting idea.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The biggest weakness is that the paper overclaims what it actually demonstrates. The proposed method is trained entirely on distortion labels, yet the paper frames the contribution as addressing broader clinical quality assessment and PI-QUAL prediction. However, PI-QUAL is a multifactorial concept, not simply a distortion label. Since the PRIME cohort is also heavily dominated by distortion-related low-quality cases, the current results mainly show that distortion-sensitive features transfer to another distortion-heavy setting. That is much narrower than the paper’s broader clinical claim. 2.The evidence for generalization to real PI-QUAL assessment is therefore limited. The paper does not show convincing analysis of non-distortion low-quality cases, so it is unclear whether the model is actually learning broader image quality or mostly detecting distortion. 3.The few-shot adaptation setting also limits practical value. The method assumes five support samples per class for adaptation, including rare low-quality cases. In realistic deployment, this requirement may still be nontrivial, especially in well-controlled clinical cohorts where low-quality scans are uncommon. The paper does not discuss this limitation in enough depth. 4.The results may be quite sensitive to support set selection, but this is not studied carefully. In few-shot learning, performance can vary substantially depending on which examples are chosen as support samples, and the current paper does not provide enough evidence that the reported gains are robust to that choice. External validation is present, but still limited. The number of low-quality and distorted cases in PRIME is small, which makes it difficult to judge how stable the conclusions would be in more diverse populations and acquisition settings. Overall, while the idea is interesting, the current empirical evidence is not strong enough to support the paper’s broader claims about clinical quality assessment.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair (AC) and Reviewers for their constructive feedback. 1.Necessity of Few-Shot Adaptation (R1) R1 argued that fully supervised learning (FSL) outperforms few-shot learning on Dataset 1 and therefore questioned the necessity of our method. Indeed, Dataset 1 is a source-domain meta-training cohort, where strong in-domain FSL performance is expected. We view this as an “oracle” upper bound requiring extensive target-domain annotations, rather than a practical solution in our intended data-constrained challenges, as in many real-world clinical applications. These require adaptation to new datasets and tasks (e.g. PRIME PI-QUAL assessment), where only a few low-quality (LQ) examples are available. In such settings, FSL becomes impractical and prone to severe overfitting, consistent with the poor FSL-5 performance on PRIME shown in Table 1.Moreover, directly applying the Dataset-1-trained FSL model to PRIME suffers from substantial domain shift caused by scanner and protocol variability across centers. This motivates few-shot learning that can transfer source-domain knowledge under clinically and practically limited target-domain supervision. 2.Expected Realistic Clinical Setting of Episodic Protocols (R1,R2,R4) We agree that, although it is still non-trivial as pointed out by the reviewer, our approach proposes a practical deployment scenario: adaptation is performed once for a new site/scanner/protocol using only five archived support scans. Non-episodic inference (R1 suggested) is certainly advantageous, but in current study, its trade-off to performance is generally poor and exemplified in Table 1. Sensitivity to a very small number (here, five) support samples (R2 and R4) is indeed the challenge that many few-shot algorithms address, also in part motivated our proposed prototypical methods designed for this challenge. Practically in our clinical workflow, the support sets are curated (instead of random sampled) to cover a b-value range of 1400–2000 and different types of LQ images (e.g. distortion vs non-distortion). However, this step was performed independently prior to experiment and as demonstrated in our experiments, yielded promising IQA performance. Related comment from R4 noted that the limited number of LQ samples in PRIME may restrict conclusions regarding stability. We emphasize that PRIME is a large-scale, highly heterogeneous multi-center dataset (483 cases across scanners/protocols/institutions). The prevalence of LQ examples therefore reflects the real clinical scenario motivating our framework. Technically, the proposed approach leverages source-domain meta-learned representations while requiring only minimal target-domain calibration, improving robustness under scarce supervision. 3.”Overclaiming” (R4) R4 noted that our model is trained on distortion labels but overclaims to solve general quality assessment. We first clarify that, in the PRIME trial, 29% of low PI-QUAL cases were associated with T2 quality issues and 87% among DWI-related quality issues were attributed to geometric distortion - a major determinant of clinical image quality in this application. More importantly, we clarify that our target is clinical, diagnosis-relevant prostate MRI quality assessment, as measured (and thus validated) by PI-QUAL, on biparametric T2 and diffusion MR from real clinical cases. In fact, the purpose of our study is to assess such a general IQA (defined for this application), but using training data only being “distortion-labelled” - by domain adaptation - because the distortion labels are much feasibly and reliably to obtain for a larger training set as demonstrated in this study.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers raise points about an extant baseline with better performance, and issues with how realistic of a clinical setting the authors’ experiment actually is. I recommend that a rebuttal address whether these concerns are correct or not. | Reviewer majority, R3 concerns seem overly critical, though valid. I find this paper to be borderline: a good method perhaps, but with clear weaknesses that remain unaddressed. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a clinically relevant and practically important problem: prostate MRI quality assessment under limited annotated data. The reviewers generally agreed that the work is technically sound, well motivated, and reasonably validated, with strengths including the distortion-aware transfer strategy, adaptation to low-data settings, and the integration of FiLM/GRL modules for robustness across acquisition settings. The study also provides external validation on a heterogeneous multi-center dataset and tackles a realistic challenge in prostate MRI quality control. The main concerns raised by reviewers focused on the scope of the claims rather than fundamental methodological flaws. In particular, reviewers questioned whether the current evidence fully supports broader claims of general PI-QUAL assessment beyond distortion-related quality degradation, and noted limited analysis of support-set sensitivity and deployment practicality. These concerns are valid and should be addressed through more careful positioning and discussion of limitations. However, the rebuttal clarified the intended use case more convincingly: the method is designed for cross-domain adaptation under severe annotation scarcity, rather than outperforming fully supervised learning in large in-domain settings. The authors also clarified the practical clinical workflow for support-set curation and the motivation for leveraging distortion labels as a scalable surrogate supervision signal. Importantly, none of the reviewers identified technical errors, invalid experiments, or major reproducibility concerns. After rebuttal, two reviewers moved to or maintained acceptance recommendations, while the remaining concerns primarily relate to claim calibration and the limited breadth of validation rather than a lack of scientific merit. Given the overall technical quality, clinical relevance, and positive reviewer consensus after rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers had split opinions, reflecting the complexity of the task. I recommend acceptance of the study based on the overall quality and reviewers comments, but I strongly encourage the authors to consider the critical points raised by the reviewers.

title: Data-Driven Optimization of Prostate Sectorization from MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: Interesting problem studied within the work; which has real clinical utility Abstract and background are very clear, with motivations summarised well Methods figure is very clear and easy to parse and most methodological details are clear/well-specified The analysis is in-depth (reporting coverage, variance and statistical tests) over the datasets
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The link to data is useful but open-sourced code to replicate the sectorization would greatly enhance reproducibility The evaluation dataset is relatively small, with just over 100 samples in total; this could be expanded; however, I do acknowledge the cost of expert time and given such constraints the size is acceptable; furthermore the authors present statistical tests, which enhance the validity of the conclusions In qualitative comparisons, it would be good to also include a radiologist’s secotrization as comparison The method assumes accurate zonal segmentation, how do errors in the zonal segmentation propagate, this could have been investigated by artificially corrupting the zonal masks; following from this a discussion on variability in training labels would also be appreciated A hyper-parameter sensitivity analysis would be extremely useful
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The main method is novel and well scoped. Instead of using a fixed rule-based script, the paper formulates prostate sectorization as a differentiable geometric optimization problem with learnable sector boundaries in a canonical coordinate space. This is interesting because it preserves interpretability and PI-RADS structure while still allowing data-driven optimization. The latent consensus loss, which is tailored to the weak-label setting. Rather than using a standard segmentation loss, the paper optimizes sector boundaries by maximizing lesion coverage within the assigned sector while penalizing spillover into lesions assigned to other sectors. This is a thoughtful formulation for noisy sector labels and lesions that may span multiple regions. The paper includes internal holdout, temporal internal, and external ProstateX cohorts, compares against both an unoptimized initialization and a prior rule-based baseline, and reports both aggregate and rule-specific performance. The work has potential downstream impact beyond the immediate task. The bidirectional bridge between sector labels and 3D MRI space could be useful for quality control, standardized data curation, and weakly supervised learning from large clinical registries.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main limitation is that the evaluation target is only an indirect proxy for correctness. Performance is measured by lesion coverage within the assigned sector, but this does not fully validate whether the learned 24-sector map is anatomically correct everywhere in the gland. A sectorization could improve lesion containment while still placing boundaries in clinically questionable locations outside lesion-bearing regions. This is especially important because the paper’s goal is standardized spatial mapping, not only lesion assignment. The experimental comparison is somewhat limited. Quantitatively, the paper compares mainly against PI-Init and one prior rule-based baseline, while Walter-Rittel et al. is discussed only qualitatively on page 7–8.Since Walter-Rittel et al. [7] is one of the most relevant prior automated 24-sector approaches cited by the paper, the lack of a direct quantitative comparison weakens the empirical case. The sector labels used for training and evaluation are weak and subjective, which the paper acknowledges. Only the main lesion sector is used even though lesions may span multiple sectors, and for ProstateX the external labels are a silver standard created specifically for this study, with annotators not blinded to the framework. The clinical claim is promising but not yet fully demonstrated. The paper argues that the framework can unlock large weakly labeled biopsy registries and support weak supervision, but this is a forward-looking application rather than something actually shown experimentally in the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper presents a novel and well-motivated formulation of prostate sectorization as a differentiable geometric problem, replacing rigid rule-based methods with a learnable and interpretable framework. The use of a canonical coordinate space and a low-dimensional parameterization enables the learning of a global anatomical prior while maintaining consistency with clinical PI-RADS definitions. The proposed objective function is well-designed for weak supervision and effectively aligns lesion locations with anatomical sectors. In addition, the evaluation is thorough, including internal, temporal, and external datasets with appropriate statistical analysis, and qualitative results demonstrate improved anatomical fidelity and consistency with clinical guidelines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper has some limitations. While the method is well-designed, the performance improvements over strong rule-based baselines are moderate and not consistently significant across all anatomical divisions, with some regions showing little to no gain. This makes it difficult to fully assess the practical impact of the proposed approach. Additionally, the framework depends on accurate zonal segmentation masks, and its performance may degrade in the presence of segmentation errors, yet this dependency is not analyzed.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Downstream weak supervision evidence (Meta-reviewer,R2). The reviewers ask whether the proposed sectorization framework translates to improved performance in downstream cancer detection. Demonstrating a full end-to-end weakly supervised cancer detection model is beyond the scope of this paper, whose contribution is the sectorization framework itself. Prior work, not published in peer-reviewed conferences, has demonstrated that lesion sector maps can be used as weak annotations for lesion localization networks (Hamzaoui’s Thesis, Chapter 5, 2023). Our contribution is improving the fidelity of that sectorization, which is a necessary prerequisite for such pipelines. To further support the data unlocking utility, we compare against the sectorization used in that prior work: our model reduces completely misaligned POST_DIV cases from 3 to 0 on ProstateX and maintains comparable rates on other datasets, while improving fully correct AP assignments on ProstateX from 23 to 35 out of 50 cases. Validation outside lesion-bearing regions (R2). The reviewer notes that lesion coverage does not fully validate sector boundaries in lesion-free regions. We are aware of the spatial sparsity of lesion coverage: lesions are not uniformly distributed in the gland, and our dataset reflects the expected imbalance (most lesions are in the mid-gland posterior sectors). Although every sector contains at least one lesion across the training set, we have explored balancing strategies (e.g., a WeightedDataLoader) but with no meaningful impact. Instead we construct our loss function to aggregate lesions into coarser anatomical regions (e.g., anterior vs. posterior), ensuring a maximum number of lesions contribute to each parameter’s optimization. Moreover, the parameters of the geometric priors governing sector boundaries are constrained by PI-RADS guidelines and initialized accordingly, preventing anatomically unrealistic solutions. Finally, providing manually annotated prostate sectors is way too expensive to obtain, and optimizing lesion coverage on a large and diverse dataset remains the best available proxy. Quantitative Comparison with Walter-Rittel (WR) (R2). A sector-level comparison with WR is not meaningful because their proposed sectors differ substantially from ours (unlike Hamzaoui’s): their method uses a coarser PZ grid that does not include the lateral-central division, which is one of our key contribution since it impacts the biopsy targeting gesture. Annotation quality and reproducibility (R2,R1). The reviewers raise concerns about annotation subjectivity and reproducibility. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first public release of prostate sector information associated with a widely used public prostate MRI dataset, ProstateX. These annotations were produced under a predefined protocol, reviewed with a senior urologist, and are publicly released to facilitate reproducibility and external validation. We believe this is a valuable contribution to the community that will first foster research on prostate image analysis. Code will be made available upon acceptance. Hyperparameter sensitivity and fixed symmetry assumptions (R1,R3). We performed ablations on the temperature parameter α and observed limited sensitivity around the selected operating point; these results were omitted due to space constraints. The symmetry assumption is inherited directly from PI-RADS topology and discussion with clinicians. Radiologist sectorization as qualitative benchmark (R1). This would be a valuable extension in future work, as manual annotation of sectors is too expensive. Robustness to zonal segmentation errors (R1,R3). Our method takes as input the zonal masks, and is dependent on their quality. The segmentation method we rely on achieves strong performance on ProstateX data (WG: 90.90±2.94, TZ: 86.84±4.33, PZ: 78.40±7.31 Dice), which motivated our decision to build on these masks rather than jointly optimize segmentation and sectorization.

title: DDecomp: Structured Uncertainty Decomposition Using Masked Autoencoders for Anomaly Detection in Diffusion MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper addresses an important and challenging problem: unsupervised anomaly detection in diffusion MRI under substantial acquisition noise and cross-protocol variability. This method is designed specifically for this problem rather than relying on reconstruction error or a generated anomaly score. The method formulation is technically sound and clearly structured, combining a healthy-data-trained masked autoencoder with heteroscedastic likelihood modelling and inference-time marginalisation over mask sampling and dropout to produce a more stable and pathology-specific uncertainty estimate. In addition, the evaluation across multiple lesion types (glioma, WMH, and ICH) and protocols shows a superior performance of the proposed method, which strengthens the practical relevance of the work.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: One concern relates to the choice of using dMRI-derived scalar map mean diffusivity (MD) as model input. The authors already mentioned that reliable lesion localisation in scalar diffusion maps remains challenging in the introduction. MD can be sensitive to various artefacts. This is an important limitation, because these derived measures are influenced not only by pathology but also by acquisition quality, preprocessing errors, and protocol variability. In practice, severe artefacts or unstable diffusion estimation may also produce abnormal intensity patterns that resemble pathology, meaning the anomaly signal may not be lesion-specific. As a result, the proposed framework may detect generic deviations from the healthy training distribution, including artefacts, noise contamination, or reconstruction failures, rather than truly pathological tissue alone. Therefore, an elevated epistemic uncertainty map may reflect either a clinically meaningful lesion or simply poor image quality. The paper would be stronger if it included a more explicit discussion or analysis of how they perform on the artefact dataset. Another weakness is the lack of clarity regarding the evaluation datasets and reproducibility. The manuscript reports experiments on glioma, intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH), and white matter hyperintensity (WMH) cohorts, but does not clearly identify the source of these datasets, provide corresponding references, or state whether they are publicly available or in-house collections. The authors also do not provide information regarding the demographics of these datasets. This makes it difficult to assess the diversity, accessibility, and potential biases of the evaluation data, and limits the reader’s ability to judge how broadly the reported results may generalise. In addition, the paper does not appear to provide any statement regarding code availability. For a method that involves several implementation-specific components, including masked autoencoding, heteroscedastic uncertainty modelling, and inference-time marginalisation, the absence of released code further reduces reproducibility. Overall, the limited transparency around both the datasets and the implementation weakens the practical reproducibility of the work.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The decomposition of the epistemic component for unsupervised anomaly detection is interesting Different lesion types have been included for comprehensive evaluation
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The methods considered for comparison were too limited The selected evaluation metrics were not sufficient
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The idea has good novelty (at least I haven’t seen normative modelling and abnormality detection done this way) I particularly like the idea of inferring the posterior on the mask by treating it as a nuisance variable.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: I don’t fully understand why high epistemic uncertainty necessarily corresponds to abnormality. There may be very common signal combinations for which epistemic uncertainty is high (e.g. where many signal combinations map to the same diffusion parameters). Not necessarily a weakness but a question: the HCP data set is predominantly “healthy” but pathologies certainly exist and are visible in the images (the website provides lists and locations). reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Uncertainty Separation (R1–3, AC): We apologize for confusion over how to separate lesions from image artifacts. Our method first estimates total uncertainty, then decomposes it into epistemic and aleatoric components via variance analysis of MC sampling and heteroscedasticity modeling. Epistemic uncertainty (measured as variance of predictive means across MC-dropout and masked samples) captures OOD from the healthy training distribution, e.g., pathological lesions with rare anatomical patterns. Image artifacts (e.g., protocol shifts, noise, and signal combinations) also shift test data from the training data characteristics, but these commonly exist across visible and masked tokens in MAE during inference, which will be captured by our heteroscedastic likelihood computation. Thus, the two uncertainties can be separated for epistemic lesion identification. Our comparison with MAE-UAD and DDEvENet shows that separating these uncertainties largely improves the identification. But, we acknowledge that our method relies on high-quality processed data and QC to exclude failures. Otherwise, severe imaging artifacts (e.g., reconstruction failures) may be recognized as epistemic OOD. Segmentation Accuracy & UAD Comparison (R2, AC): (1) We will clarify that Fβ (Tab. 1) quantifies segmentation accuracy by measuring the similarity between binary lesion masks (by thresholding the anomaly scores) and manual segmentation. (2) Due to space limit, our current work compared two most relevant approaches: MAE-UAD (a reconstruction-error method from the same MAE family as ours) and DDEvENet (an uncertainty estimation method designed for dMRI on the same task and data as ours). We agree that including more UAD methods will strengthen our evaluation, and will expand to discuss these work and include comparisons in future journal extension. Abnormalities in Training (R3, AC): We confirm that no cases were excluded due to pathologies during training, and acknowledge that incidental abnormalities may be present when learning the healthy population normative model. As such cases are rare and spatially sparse relative to normal whole‑brain tissue, they will cause limited contamination rather than deviating the learned normative model. Moreover, our random masking design further prevents such contamination because abnormal regions form a small fraction of visible token targets. The heteroscedastic likelihood will also assign higher variance to such isolated high-residual observations, reducing their effects on the learned mean. Identifying such cases in the training set would require further investigation into abnormal data characteristics, which is beyond the scope of this work. But we believe these abnormalities would be detected as they lie outside the learned normative distribution. Data Transparency and Code (R1, AC): Due to the anonymous policy, we did not include source of our in‑house clinical data. Upon acceptance, we will add data details, including demographics and clinical characteristics. Further, we confirm that the code and trained weights will be released. Beyond dMRI (R2, AC): AC and R2 are correct that our method can be generally applied to other modalities. We will clarify that it is a general uncertainty-decomposition framework, not task-specific. This work focuses on dMRI as it’s a natural application for separating aleatoric variability from epistemic OOD response due to its inherent variation from acquisitions, scanner differences, and microstructural pathology. Computation Efficiency (R2): Our method requires K (# of random masks, 100) x T (# of MC-dropout samples, 10) forward passes for inference, which takes ~2 min per subject. Expanded Discussion (R3): As suggested, we will expand Discussion to include limitations regarding severe artifact effects, reliance on high-quality processed data, potential abnormalities in the training data, and future work on testing beyond dMRI as well as comparisons with more UAD methods.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This manuscript proposes a masked autoencoder based framework for anomaly detection in diffusion MRI that decomposes predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. Reviewers thought that this was an interesting and innovative approach to a relevant and challenging problem, and yielded promising qualitative results. However, they also raised a number of concerns that are too serious to directly recommend acceptance. It would be helpful if authors could comment on them in their rebuttal, keeping in mind that no new results are permitted at this point: 1.All reviewers questioned how helpful and reliable the separation between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty really is for separating lesions from other abnormalities such as image artifacts. They thought that this was not demonstrated clearly enough. 2.The accuracy of the proposed approach as a lesion segmentation tool has not been quantified, and reviewers missed a comparison to multiple plausible baselines for anomaly detection. 3.It is unclear how abnormalities in the HCP training data have been handled. 4.The sources and characteristics of the clinical data used in this work are not sufficiently transparent. 5.Reviewers expressed doubt that, without making source code available, it will be possible to reproduce this work. 6.It is not clear why the authors focus on diffusion MRI, since the method should be more widely applicable. | Some limitations remain after rebuttal and should be clearly stated in the final version of the paper, in particular, assumptions regarding image quality that underlie the proposed separation between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, and assumptions regarding effects of training data contamination being negligible. Concerns regarding reproducibility have been addressed by promising the release of code and model weights along with the paper. Authors are encouraged to include additional information about selection of anomaly score threshold and stability of results w.r.t. this choice, which is a major remaining concern. Despite this, I agree with the positive reviewer majority vote after rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The uncertainty decomposition idea is genuinely novel and the dMRI application is well-motivated. However, the UAD field offers a substantial number of directly applicable methods and situating the contribution in this context is not optional. Adding baseline comparisons requires only additional rows in a table and deferring this to a journal extension is not an appropriate rebuttal response. The claimed improvements cannot be properly assessed without this context. Additionally, no dataset information is provided beyond lesion type, including sources, demographics, or acquisition protocols. This is feasible even under anonymity and its absence makes it impossible to assess generalizability, site bias, or protocol dependence for a method that explicitly claims robustness across these factors. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I am choosing to accept this paper, but I do agree with one of the points raised by R2, that the experimental baselines are disappointing. Still, it is innovative and interesting, and with 2 vs 1 it becomes editorial choice.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank reviewers for their constructive comments. [R1] Reference links Fixed. [R1] Worth exploring … sparse single-shell acquisition We explored sparse source directions in Cam-CAN. For PSNR/SSIM/RMSE/ΔFA/ΔMD, 15 directions give 28.7/0.966/0.028/0.039/0.49, while 6 directions give 27.7/0.959/0.035/0.047/0.58, showing stable performance under moderate sparsity and gradual degradation as expected. [R1] Figure presentation Thank you for pointing out the typo in Fig. 2.We only use dMRI and DTI priors, and will replace the misleading T1 patch with an SH coefficient patch. [R2] Motivation: Why synthesize multi-shell instead of directly predicting NODDI? Multi-shell synthesis is more flexible than predicting one specific map. The synthesized shell can support multiple analyses beyond NODDI, e.g. DTI, DKI and free-water imaging, whereas a NODDI-specific model is less reusable. We will clarify this motivation. [R2] Weak contribution vs. [4] (DirUNet) We respectfully disagree. [4] is not an SH-CNN; it performs low-to-high b-value regression in raw volume space and uses nearest-direction matching for unpaired directions. In contrast, we regress in the SH domain, enabling synthesis for arbitrary target directions. We further introduce direction-agnostic DTI conditioning and signal-consistency regularization to address ambiguity and signal fidelity in SH regression. [R2] More advanced architectures, such as attention-based blocks We partially agree that advanced modules may further improve performance. To examine this, we tested bottleneck spatial self-attention on a Cam-CAN subset, which slightly improved the results from 28.9/0.968/0.027/0.036/0.44 to 29.1/0.969/0.025/0.033/0.44, but increased parameters by 4.7% and required more 3D memory. Thus, we believe the current design provides a simple yet reasonable trade-off. We will explore advanced architectures in future work. [R2] Compare purely synthesised to pure GT, and quantitative evaluation for NODDI maps We agree and will add quantitative NODDI evaluation in revision. Regarding evaluation bias, our downstream evaluation already follows [4]: the acquired source shell and synthesized high-b shell form the synthesized multi-shell dMRI for downstream evaluation. This matches the intended case, where only the missing high-b shell is synthesized. Since NODDI requires multi-shell dMRI, evaluating only the synthesized high-b shell is not applicable. [R2] Don’t use Comic Sans font Fixed. [R3] Competitive DirUNet performance on UKB This is mainly due to the 50 source directions in UKB, as DirUNet’s nearest-direction matching benefits from dense references. In 6-direction UKB experiments, visual drops are similar for DTI-SHNet and DirUNet: 0.5/1.4/0.014 vs. 0.5/1.6/0.011 in PSNR/SSIM/RMSE. However, downstream drops are smaller for DTI-SHNet: 0.014/0.08 vs. DirUNet’s 0.035/0.40 in ΔFA/ΔMD, suggesting better robustness under sparse directions. [R3] Cam-CAN vs. UKB gap The gap is due to data distribution, not size alone. With matched-size training subsets of 200 subjects, the gap remains in our model, with differences of 3.8/4.7/0.059/0.005/0.10.This suggests gradient directions and cohort difference are major factors. [R3] Center crop and patch training Center cropping standardizes scans to a unified shape while preserving the whole brain. Patch training improves memory efficiency and augmentation for 3D regression, as in nnU-Net and 3D MedDiffusion. Full-volume inference uses overlapping sliding windows. [R3] Quantitative analysis on NODDI We will add quantitative NODDI errors in revision. [R3] Reproducibility details We will add the brain-mask definition, preprocessing references, train/test split, epochs, and training details. Fixed epochs are chosen from preliminary convergence experiments without using the test set. Final checkpoints are evaluated. [R3] Fixed b-value pair limitation We agree that the current model is trained for a fixed mapping, and will discuss carefully.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews show clear disagreement: one strong accept contrasts with a firm reject citing weak motivation and unconvincing results, while another leans weak accept with noted concerns. Given this variance, a rebuttal is necessary to clarify the paper’s clinical/methodological motivation and to strengthen the evidence supporting the reported improvements. The authors should particularly address concerns about the significance and robustness of results, and better justify the novelty and practical impact of the proposed method. | All reviewers recommended acceptance.
