Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Significant concerns could be addressed and were well received by two of the reviewers. The presented deep learning model for synthesizing multi-shell diffusion MRI from single-shell dMRI has the strengths of a novel methodological contribution for a key problem (allowing advanced dMRI analysis with short scans), comprehensive comparison and a well written, clear manuscript - which now that other concerns were addressed - might result in positive discussions and stimulating poster conversations. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The authors have produced a technically sound piece of work that addresses an important problem in dMRI analysis. However, the marginal improvements over existing methods and the lack of compelling clinical and methodological justification mean that the paper does not meet the rigorous standards required for acceptance at MICCAI. While the authors have effectively addressed all major technical concerns from the review process and clarified aspects of the method’s novelty and practicality, the paper still falls short of MICCAI’s high acceptance standards. MICCAI requires submissions to demonstrate significant contributions that advance the state-of-the-art in medical image computing and computer-assisted intervention. In this case, the marginal performance improvements and unresolved motivation issues prevent the paper from meeting this bar. It is also important to note that, per MICCAI guidelines, the rebuttal should not introduce new experimental results. Based on the above evaluation, I recommend rejection of this paper. I encourage the authors to strengthen the motivation for their approach, conduct more extensive comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, and explore additional clinical applications to demonstrate the practical value of their work for future submissions.

title: DynFS-MoE: Dynamic Functional-Structural Mixture-of-Experts for Post-Traumatic Epilepsy Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.sMRI can leverage a temporal MoE mechanism to select the most informative patches within fMRI segments for cross-modal fusion and routing. 2.Modality-specific experts are employed to extract individual feature representations from each modality, producing dedicated embeddings that preserve modality-unique information. 3.A class-based MoE module adaptively selects the most class-relevant modality patches to facilitate more discriminative classification.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The number of subjects in the dataset is relatively small, with only around 20 samples for each type. Will this affect the validity of the results? Should a larger dataset be used to validate the findings? 2.More state-of-the-art methods should be included in the comparative experiments for model performance evaluation. 3.In addition to discussing binary classification problems, is it feasible to apply the model to a three-class classification task that distinguishes among HC, TBI and PTE? 4.The text in Figure 2 is too small and should be optimized for better readability. 5.A more comprehensive ablation study is recommended.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The MCoE module is a significant innovation in this paper. Unlike standard MoEs that route solely based on input features, MCoE constructs the routing logits as a 3D tensor, explicitly introducing the conditional constraint of “disease class”. This allows the model to dynamically adjust its reliance on different modalities according to different disease phenotypes. 2.The interpretability analysis is exceptionally well-executed and aligns perfectly with clinical logic. The derived routing weights compellingly demonstrate that TBI diagnosis heavily relies on static structural connectivity (sMRI), whereas PTE diagnosis cleverly down-weights the reliance on sMRI and shifts focus to dynamic functional abnormal discharges in early/mid-temporal segments (S2-S4). Furthermore, the ROI interaction heatmaps reveal progressive “frontal-occipital” abnormal connectivity unique to PTE, which is highly consistent with existing neuropathological literature. 3.Utilizing scaled dot-product attention to inject global sMRI structural priors into local fMRI temporal patches via residual connections is a lightweight yet highly effective strategy. This cleverly mitigates modality competition prior to entering the MoE routing layer.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Critically Small Dataset and High Overfitting Risk: The entire study is based on only 69 subjects (26 HC, 24 TBI, 19 PTE). Training an MoE architecture containing complex routing mechanisms and regularizations on such a tiny dataset is highly susceptible to severe overfitting. 2.Severe Disconnect Between Figures and Text: There is a confusing disconnect between the framework diagram and the textual description. For instance, Section 2.4 specifies that the input to MCoE incorporates both cross-modal fusion and modality-specific processing from prior layers, but in Figure 1, the input to MCoE appears to solely come from the cross-modal fusion path, demonstrating a clear inconsistency. 3.Lack of Explicit Mathematical Constraints for “Modality-Specific” MSoE: In Section 2.3, the authors claim that MSoE extracts “modality-specific features”. However, structurally, MSoE is merely a standard MoE layer. The paper lacks any explicit loss function or physical isolation to force a certain expert to “only process fMRI” or “only process sMRI”; it relies entirely on data-driven learning. 4.Missing Unimodal Baselines and Key Ablation Details: Since one of the paper’s claimed innovations is that “dynamic multimodal fusion is superior to unimodal methods,” comparisons with unimodal baseline models must be included. Moreover, the current ablation study only verifies the routing strategy, lacking a systematic component-wise ablation of the core modules.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Develops a time-aware functional-structural encoder that partitions fMRI into temporal segments and uses scaled dot-product attention to integrate structural connectivity features; MoE-based dynamic modality fusion; strong performance on a clinical dataset; A Brain Interpretability Regularizer based on conditional mutual information is used to reveal disease-specific brain interaction patterns.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The study relies on a very small cohort of 69 subjects, which raises significant concerns about the robustness and generalizability. The paper lacks a comparison against a standard multimodal fusion baseline, such as simple feature concatenation, to isolate the specific benefit of the MoE routing; he paper does not report $p$-values or formal statistical significance tests to confirm that the improvements over baselines are statistically robust.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: General Response[R1,R2,R3]: We sincerely thank the AC and reviewers for their constructive comments. Sample Size Issue:We spent 4 years collecting this dataset because PTE is a relatively rare neurological disorder requiring long-term follow-up for definitive diagnosis. Acquiring both fMRI and DTI data is also costly, while preprocessing and manual curation are highly time-consuming. Existing studies used similarly limited cohorts: [1] included 24 HC and 22 TBI subjects [2] included HC: n=13, TBI: n=16, and TBI converters/seizure group: n=17.To our paper survey, no prior study has simultaneously included larger TBI and PTE cohorts with both fMRI and DTI modalities. Moreover, our work is the first to jointly investigate fMRI and DTI for TBI/PTE-related epilepsy using a deep learning framework. [1] Kang et al. (2025), Relationship Between Structural and Functional Network Connectivity Changes for Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury and Chronic Health Symptoms. [2] Raizman et al. (2020), Traumatic Brain Injury Severity in a Network Perspective: A Diffusion MRI–Based Connectome Study. Overfitting in Small Samples [R2]:To mitigate overfitting in a relatively small dataset, we adopt a lightweight MoE with class-conditioned dynamic routing instead of a large dense architecture, activating only selected experts per sample to control effective capacity. We further apply conditional mutual information regularization to constrain modality–expert routing, improving stability. DynFS-MoE consistently improved performance, while ablation studies confirmed the importance of class-conditioned routing. Comparison with Unimodal Methods and Statistical Significance [R2,R3]: Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we conducted Welch’s t-test between DynFS-MoE and the best baseline methods. For HC vs. PTE, DynFS-MoE improved ACC, AUC, and F1-score by 5.0%, 7.7%, and 9.5%, respectively. Improvements in AUC and F1-score were highly significant (p<0.001), while ACC also achieved significance (p<0.05). Compared with the best unimodal models (fMRI-FC MLP or sMRI MLP), DynFS-MoE further improved AUC and F1-score by 15.1% and 11.0%. For TBI vs. PTE, DynFS-MoE improved ACC by 6.9% and AUC by 22.4% over the best baseline, both with high significance (p<0.001). We also compared our approach with recent SOTA models, including MultiViT (2024), IBrainGNN (2025), and AGIIBM (2025). DynFS-MoE consistently outperformed competing methods across all cohorts, achieving ACC gains of 2.7%, 7.7%, and 10.0%, respectively. [R1-2]In addition, DynFS-MoE (AUC=0.67) can flexibly support 3-class classification and achieves an average improvement of 2.41% across 3-class classification tasks. Figure–Text Inconsistency[R2]: [R2-2] We thank the reviewer for identifying the inconsistency between Fig. 1 and Section~2.4, and we will revise the arrow connection to MCoE in Fig.1.Section~2.4 states that the input to the MCoE is the refined modality patch embeddings $Z={z_i} {i=1}^{|P|}$ after cross-modal fusion and modality-specific processing. Each $z_i$ incorporates both the cross-modal fusion outputs from Section~2.2 ($\tilde{f}^{(k)}$, $z {\text{fused}}^{(k)}$) and the MSoE outputs from Section~2.3.Therefore, MCoE operates on joint representations containing both cross-modal interactions and modality-specific specialization. [R2-3] In the MSoE module, fMRI (color blocks) and sMRI (red-highlighted blocks) are already represented as modality-specific inputs. Specialization arises from the modality-defined patch space, routing mechanism, and class-conditioned dispatch. Specifically, DynFS-MoE constructs modality patches $P={f^{(1)},\dots,f^{(K)},s}$ and routes them through $P_\theta(E=e_j\mid P=p_i)$, enabling experts to specialize to different modality distributions. In addition, the class-conditioned routing and conditional mutual information regularizer $I(P;E\mid Y)$ encourage modality- and class-dependent expert associations instead of uniform expert sharing.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The three reviewers offer a mixed overall recommendation, with two weak accepts and one weak reject. They confirmed the novel DynFS-MoE framework for its dynamic, class-conditioned routing and clinically meaningful interpretability, but unanimously raise serious concerns about the extremely small cohort (only 69 subjects) that heightens overfitting risk and limits generalizability. Further shared weaknesses include the absence of unimodal and simple fusion baselines, a lack of statistical significance testing, inconsistencies between text and figures, and insufficient ablation studies. The authors should prepare the rebuttal to address those concerns. | After considering the initial reviews, the authors’ rebuttal, and the updated reviewer assessments, the paper is recommended for acceptance. The reviewers acknowledged the novelty of the DynFS-MoE framework and its clinically meaningful interpretability. The authors also addressed the reviewers’ concerns in the rebuttal by providing statistical tests that confirmed significant improvements over baselines, clarifying the framework’s design and correcting the figure inconsistency, and justifying the dataset size by the clinical rarity of post-traumatic epilepsy. The work’s dynamic class-conditioned routing and multimodal fusion, despite the data limitations, are seen as sufficiently valuable for publication. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two reviewers (Weak Reject, Weak Accept) did not submit post-rebuttal assessments. The third reviewer recommends to accept this paper. I share this assessment. Reviewers appreciated particularly the methodological contribution of this work paired with the conducted (interpretability) analyses. A shared main criticism centred around the small sample size of the dataset. However, I agree with the authors that acquiring a suitable, large dataset is challenging, given the application. I consider the provided evidence as sufficient and would down-weight this critique. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper contributes a clinically motivated dynamic functional-structural mixture-of-experts framework for post-traumatic epilepsy diagnosis, with a sensible attempt to combine heterogeneous signals in a difficult small-sample setting. The rebuttal seems to have clarified the design motivation and the overfitting-mitigation perspective, which keeps the paper acceptable after rebuttal.

title: Explainability in Multimodal Deep Transformation Models for Stroke Outcome Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Strong Focus on Trustworthy AI: The paper’s greatest strength is that it tackles the critical issue of explainability head-on. Instead of merely chasing a higher AUC, it focuses on making the model’s decisions transparent, which is paramount for building trust and facilitating the clinical adoption of AI. 2.Highly Insightful and Compelling Analysis: The analysis demonstrating that the model’s visual attention shifts away from age-related brain regions once ‘age’ is explicitly included as a tabular predictor is a standout finding. This provides powerful, concrete evidence that the proposed XAI framework is effective at revealing the model’s internal reasoning. 3.Intelligent Model Design (dTMs): The choice of Deep Transformation Models (dTMs) is perfectly aligned with the paper’s goals. This hybrid approach elegantly combines the interpretive power of statistical models for tabular data with the feature extraction capabilities of deep learning for imaging data. 4.Systematic Error and Hypothesis Analysis: The use of t-SNE to cluster explanation maps reveals distinct spatial patterns associated with correct and incorrect predictions. This is an excellent example of how the framework can be used for systematic error analysis, helping researchers understand not just when the model fails, but potentially why.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Marginal Predictive Gain from Imaging Data: The multi-modal model (AUC 0.812) showed almost no performance improvement over the clinical-only model (AUC 0.809). This strongly suggests that the complex 3D CNN imaging branch provided little to no additional predictive value. While the paper’s focus is on explainability, this lack of predictive gain is a significant weakness regarding the clinical utility of the imaging component. 2.Lack of External Validation and Limited Sample Size: The study was conducted on a cohort of 407 patients from a single institution. This limits the generalizability of the findings, as the model’s performance and the stability of its explanations have not been tested on external data from other centers with different patient populations or imaging protocols. 3.Inherent Limitations of Post-hoc XAI: The paper relies on post-hoc explanation methods like Grad-CAM. It is important to acknowledge that these methods provide an approximation of the model’s behavior and are not a substitute for inherently interpretable models. The paper could have benefited from a more thorough discussion of the potential pitfalls and limitations of relying on such post-hoc techniques for high-stakes decisions.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The major strength of this paper is the use of a unified framework to “control” for demographic/clinical tabular data when generating explainability maps from 3D CNNs. This is a gap that needs addressed and has widespread applicability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are several weaknesses in this work. First, the model performance is pretty poor considering the outcome of interest was binary mRS (0-2,3-5). This might be due to class imbalance, which was never explicitly addressed by the authors. Second, there are inconsistencies throughout the paper. For example, in the abstract it states that age was the variable that made the maps “disappear”, but in the paper the authors report that pre-mRS and NIHSS were the major confounds, which is more reasonable. They also did not mention controlling for stroke volume, which is known to be a strong predictor of outcome. Third, the maps presented in Figures 3 and 4 are just not convincing. They all look like noise with no spatial specificity. Stronger justification and explanation for why these maps are useful would make the paper much stronger. Fourth, the authors chose 10-fold CV instead of a held-out test set to validate their findings. With 407 patients, it seems that a small held-out test set could have been utilized for better validation.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The work is relevance and very useful, and could be promising for clinical data interpretation, as it developed deep transformation models to predict functional independence three months after stroke using DWI scans from 407 patients. The work enhances the interpretability of the medical data as clinical insights regarding the functional independence before stroke and stroke severity on admission can be gained, as this serves as a great biomarkers for stroke pathophysiology. This is a great and very interesting work. Even though, the architectural design is not mathematical, and lack fundamental knowledge, the whole concept, clinical usefulness, and relevance is of great importance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The author should define al the symbols and notations and remove all typos. Overall, the work is in good shape, and the trajectory of training should be well stated, and all other parameters should be clearly defined for reproducibility.
reviewer_3_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for acknowledging our contributions to explainable AI through the integration of xAI methods into deep transformation models. Predictive Power and Clinical Endpoint (R1, R2): As noted by R1 and R2, the models show an AUC of approximately 0.8, with limited predictive gain when adding imaging to clinical data. However, this is consistent with other multimodal approaches that report AUC values between 0.65 and 0.8 in acute ischemic stroke. This is assumed to be attributed to unpredictable post-stroke events (e.g., recurrent strokes), that directly influence 3-month functional outcome (mRS). Further, we consider the modest gain in prediction performance when adding imaging to tabular data to be a clinical finding rather than a model failure. In experimental settings, neurologists also showed limited performance gain when being provided with additional imaging data, settings in which our deep transformation models outperformed them. We agree that we have missed to include this in the discussion section and will add more context in the final version. Consistency of Imaging Findings (R2): We want to respectfully point out that there is no inconsistency between the abstract and the reported findings. The image-only model uses brain regions such as frontal lobe as a surrogate for age, which is known to be an important predictor for 3-month mRS. One of the most important findings – praised by R1 – is that the highlighting of this age-related brain region disappears once age is provided explicitly as a tabular feature. The fact that admission NIHSS and pre-stroke mRS are primary drivers for 3-month mRS prediction does not contradict the observation that imaging-only models focus on age, since NIHSS and pre-stroke mRS are clinical factors that seem to have no specific surrogate brain region that could be highlighted by the xAI maps. We will explain this more clearly in the revised manuscript. Generalizability and Study Scope (R1, R3): As acknowledged by R1, the primary focus of this paper is on introducing explainability to a novel multimodal architecture. We agree with R3 that the novelty of the xAI methods (Grad-CAM, Occlusion) is modest; however, we chose these well-established methods as a reliable benchmark for the first application of xAI to our framework before moving to more complex techniques in future work. We agree with R1 that our single-center cohort of 407 patients limits generalizability and that external validation remains a necessary next step, which will be addressed in the future. We will add these limitations to the discussion section. Validation Strategy, Class Imbalance, and Training (R2): With 407 patients, a single held-out test set (e.g., 15%) would yield performance estimates that are highly sensitive to the specific random split, especially for the lower frequency class. Therefore, we implemented a strict nested setup: hyperparameter tuning and model selection were performed exclusively on internal validation splits, keeping each test fold entirely unseen and untouched during the training and tuning phases. This approach utilizes the full dataset for evaluation and provides a more reliable estimate of generalizability than a single split. A detailed description of the training procedure and the tuning parameters is provided in Figure 2 and highlighted in the manuscript. Further, as indicated in the manuscript, the code will be published on GitHub for full reproducibility. Quality of xAI Maps (R2, R3): R2 indicated that the maps appear noisy; however, our t-SNE cluster analysis demonstrates that these maps contain non-random spatial patterns correlating with correct vs. incorrect predictions and identifying predictive brain regions (e.g. frontal lobe region as surrogate for age) which provide honest transparency, as R1 highlighted. We further provide a link to an interactive t-SNE plot and highlight identified spatial patterns in Figure 4.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper provides a clinically valuable framework for explainable multi-modal stroke outcome prediction. All reviewers recognize the contribution to trustworthy medical AI but with mixed review for the paper: two support acceptance for its high-quality XAI analysis and one recommends rejection due to weak predictive performance and unconvincing visualization. I opt for Invite for Rebuttal such that the authors can clarify the concerns raised by the reviewers. | The reviewers' concerns are addressed with the exception of generalisability and robustness, given the single-centre nature of the study. However, the study focuses on explainability, and from this point of view, the amendments that the authors commit to carry out, address the weaknesses mentioned by the three reviewers. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Despite some valid concerns about, e.g., the modest predictive gain from imaging data and the lack of external validation, the explainability-focused contribution of this paper is valuable. The work provides a useful framework for interrogating multimodal stroke outcome models and may stimulate valuable discussions at MICCAI. I therefore recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clearly addresses the concerns mainly raised by one of the reviewers. Especially, the validation strategy is well-motivated and thought through which is commendable. As the concerns are succesfully rebutted and the two other reviewers were positive, I recomment to accept this work.

title: Feature Space Guidance for Breast Cancer Classification in DCE-MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: The CURIAtor module introduces a solution to temporal sampling variability by dynamically selecting the most informative post-contrast phase based on feature-space dissimilarity, it bypasses the limitations and biases of static phase selection rules. The validation pipeline is strong through utilizing leave-one-center-out cross-validation across five distinct clinical centers, alongside an entirely unseen multi-site dataset (AMBL), and provides a highly realistic assessment of out-of-distribution generalizability. By specifically addressing the heterogeneity of acquisition protocols (varying temporal resolution, number of phases, and contrast timing) across different clinical sites, the method targets a major barrier to the deployment of automated DCE-MRI screening tools.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the reported performance gains are substantial (e. g. , an 8 AUROC point improvement over MIP baselines), the paper currently lacks statistical significance testing for the results presented in Table 1.Could the authors incorporate more statistical tests to validate the robustness of these multi-center improvements? The ablation study in Table 2 effectively demonstrates the value of the adaptive CURIAtor module compared to fixed temporal combinations (e. g. , Pre + Post1 + Post2). However, how does this 3-phase selection approach compare against standard sequence modeling baselines (such as recurrent networks, 3D+t convolutions, or temporal transformers) designed to natively process the entirety of the 4D sequence? While the paper excellently evaluates center-level protocol shifts, there is no breakdown of model performance across different tumor characteristics. Can the authors discuss whether the proposed adaptive temporal sampling maintains consistent sensitivity across varying lesion sizes, morphological types (e. g. , mass vs. non-mass enhancement), or molecular subtypes?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.One major strength of this work is its clinical relevance. Robust classification on multi-center breast DCE MRI is an important and challenging task, and this study directly addresses highly practical issues, especially protocol heterogeneity across centers and the sparsity of small lesions relative to the full image volume. 2.The paper is generally clearly written and well organized. The proposed framework is conceptually coherent, with a clear internal structure: it first reduces irrelevant background through anatomically informed ROI extraction, then addresses temporal heterogeneity through adaptive phase selection, and finally improves downstream classification through large-scale lesion-aware pretraining. This multi-stage design is well motivated and easy to follow. 3.The reported experimental results are promising and support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The model shows performance advantages over several compared baselines. In addition, the paper states that the method achieved first place in the corresponding MICCAI challenge, which further suggests the competitiveness and potential practical value of the approach.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The dataset description is insufficient. The manuscript does not clearly describe the class distribution of the three categories, and in particular, it lacks detailed statistics on scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, and center-specific differences. For a paper whose main objective is cross-center generalization, these details are essential. Requiring readers to search for this information elsewhere is not helpful and weakens the clarity and completeness of the study. 2.The core rationale behind the adaptive temporal selection module has not been fully validated. The method selects the post-contrast phase that is most dissimilar to the first post-contrast phase in latent feature space. Still, the paper does not sufficiently demonstrate that this phase is truly the most clinically informative. Although Figure 2 provides three examples, it would be much more intuitive if these examples were directly matched with the actual MR images from the corresponding time points. I assume a large distance in feature space may reflect meaningful delayed washout information, but it could also arise from noise, motion artifacts, registration error, or scanner induced domain shift. In particular, Figure 2 raises a question: for the three illustrated cases, why is the final time point not the most dissimilar one? In DCE MRI, contrast enhancement typically evolves over time, so one might expect the difference to increase gradually. Additional explanation and more intuitive visualization with real DCE MRI images would strengthen the argument. 3.The implementation details of the foundation model baselines remain unclear. The paper compares against Merlin, VISTA3D, CT FM, and Curia as finetuned FM baselines, but it is not clear how these models were finetuned, whether any layers were frozen, and whether they used the same input setting as the proposed method. In addition, several of these models were originally developed for CT rather than breast MRI. Furthermore, Table 2 appears questionable. It reports mean values across datasets, but the reported mean AUROC of 74.89 is identical to the AMBL AUROC in Table 1, rather than the overall mean, maybe an error/typo? Please check this carefully. It would also be more informative if Table 2, like Table 1, reported center-specific results rather than only aggregated values.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The choice of the adequate MRI sequences is not obvious, especially when the protocols vary. An automated selection of the sequences may be relevant not only in breast, but in other modalities as well. The paper is generally clear and the ablations illustrate the advantages of the proposed method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper seems to lack the context of the state of the art. Not much is said about the Odelia Challenge and the winners (https://odelia2025.grand-challenge.org/odelia-breast-mri-challenge-2025-winners/). This makes it difficult to position the method. With that, it seems to have limited contribution with regard to the performances increase. For instance, other works (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.27326) allow to achieve higher scores.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that they recognized the clinical relevance (R2, R3), the novelty of the adaptive CURIAtor module (R1, R3), the rigor of our multi-center evaluation (R1, R2), and the manuscript’s clarity (R1, R2, R3). The points raised are actionable and primarily concern contextualization, statistical reporting, and explanatory detail rather than the validity of the framework or the multi-center results: @R3 Positioning We agree the ODELIA challenge context should be clearer. The cited arXiv work is a preliminary unpublished challenge write-up covering the pretraining and ROI-separation components of the present framework under static phase configuration; that configuration is precisely reflected in the Pre+P1+P2 ablation row in our Table 2, which our full framework (with adaptive CURIAtor phase selection) outperforms by 4.86 AUROC and 1.66 BA points. In that prior work, AMBL was part of the training set, and the resulting numbers are therefore not fully comparable to our six-cohort mean evaluation, in which AMBL is fully held out. Scores higher than our mean evaluation are single-fold ablation values solely on CAM, in line with our CAM fold results. @R1 Statistical testing We performed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all methods; summarized here ours against the strongest baseline (MIP): AUROC: 75.36 [72.25, 78.29] vs. 67.38 [64.63, 69.95]; BA: 65.78 [63.16, 66.68] vs. 60.42 [58.46, 62.42]. Both improvements are statistically significant. Fold-level CIs for all methods will be added to Table 1. @R1 Subgroup analysis Unfortunately the cohorts lack harmonized subgroup metadata: ODELIA is labeled at the breast/exam level without lesion sizes, morphology, or molecular subtype annotations, and AMBL provides richer pathology data only for a subset. We will note this limitation. @R2 Dataset details We will include a concise summary of dataset characteristics and class distributions in the manuscript. @R2 CURIAtor rationale and validation DCE-MRI kinetics may show wash-in, plateau, or washout, so the final phase is not necessarily the most dissimilar from P1, accounting for the cases in Fig. 2.CURIAtor uses P1 as a clinically motivated anchor and selects the phase most complementary in latent space, not merely the most temporally distant. Table 2’s static ablations show the adaptive choice outperforms fixed last- and mid-phase variants, indicating the selected phase is genuinely more informative. To reduce the risk that dissimilarity reflects noise, motion, registration, or scanner shifts, distances are computed after breast cropping and weighted by pooled ROI-token overlap. We will extend Fig. 2 with the corresponding MRI slices. @R2 FM baselines & Table 2 All non-CURIA baselines were fine-tuned end-to-end with input resolution and CURIAtor-selected inputs matched to our method; We used AdamW with a cosine schedule (100 epochs, batch 32, 50 steps/epoch). For CURIA: Frozen 2D embeddings, slice-wise mean aggregation and linear probe. Results indicate that CT-only FMs perform as well as CT+MRI FM. R2 is correct that the Table 2 value duplicates the AMBL column from Table 1; we will correct it and add further implementation details. @R1 Native 4D models Native 4D models constitute a research direction of their own, beyond the rebuttal window and out of scope here, where we target improvements within the prevailing fixed-input paradigm. Post-contrast phases each relate to pre-contrast and have bidirectional dependencies with one another; variable phase counts and timings require interpolation, padding, or protocol-specific resampling, each a temporal prior that confounds model vs. harmonization gains; challenges compounded by small cohorts and high VRAM costs. The field reflects this: the ODELIA challenge had no temporal entries, and in MAMA-MIA the only temporal architecture used a fixed 3-phase input. We will more explicitly position 4D modeling as future work.

title: HAM-BGT: Harmonic-Aware Multimodal Brain Graph Transformer for Brain Disease Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The approach is highly interesting, introducing a novel method to explicitly combine DTI-derived structural harmonics with functional features. 2.The experimental validation is thorough, demonstrating the framework’s effectiveness across multiple public datasets (ADNI and ABIDE) against strong baselines. 3.The manuscript is clearly written and logically structured, making the complex connectome-harmonic concepts and the proposed architecture easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.he proposed framework introduces several crucial hyperparameters, yet there is no comprehensive sensitivity analysis. 2.The ABIDE dataset subset utilized in the experiments contains only 95 subjects. Given that Transformer-based architectures are inherently data-hungry and prone to overfitting on small datasets, evaluating such a highly parameterized model on a small cohort raises concerns regarding the robustness and true generalizability of the reported results. 3.In Section 3.4, the authors identify the top 10 most discriminative ROIs for each diagnostic task using a t-test. However, the specific implementation details of this statistical analysis are currently insufficient.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Genuinely novel and theoretically grounded perspective that advances the field. Connectome harmonics theory [Atasoy et al., Nature Neuroscience 2016] — where structural connectivity eigenmodes form a Fourier-like basis constraining functional dynamics — is a well-established neuroscience framework that has not been computationally exploited in the deep learning community for brain disease diagnosis. This paper offers the first systematic bridge between this theoretical framework and practical disease classification. Unlike the other papers in this batch that combine known components, HAM-BGT introduces a fundamentally new computational lens for multimodal brain network modeling. This represents a genuine contribution to the MICCAI community. Technically sound and physically interpretable module design. (a) SGFBHE (Eq. 1-4): The radial basis filters h_i(λ) (Eq. 2) at each eigenvalue λ_i function as band-pass filters isolating harmonic-specific structural patterns. The binarized anatomical mask Ã_s (Eq. 3) suppresses spectral leakage along verified pathways — this is more physically principled than standard Laplacian positional encoding because it explicitly constrains information flow to anatomically verified connections. (b) Harmonic-Aware Filter (Eq. 6-8): The GFT→spectral filtering→IGFT pipeline is a well-defined signal processing operation applied in the connectome-harmonic domain. The combination of Gaussian smearing for smooth filter response and Tukey windowing for spectral truncation artifact suppression is technically well-motivated. (c) The gating mechanism f_{θ1} before GFT provides node-wise adaptivity, allowing different ROIs to have different spectral responses — this is important as different brain regions may contribute differently to different harmonic modes. The most comprehensive and convincing experimental evaluation among the reviewed papers. (a) Four diagnostic tasks spanning two datasets (ABIDE: ASD vs. NC; ADNI: AD vs. NC, AD vs. MCI, MCI vs. NC). (b) Nine baseline methods including recent strong baselines from top venues: ALTER (NeurIPS 2024), BrainNetTF (NeurIPS 2022), Cross-GNN (TMI 2023), MME-GCN (MedIA 2022). (c) Table 1 results show consistent and substantial margins: ASD vs. NC: 78.9% ACC (+5.1% over best multimodal baseline MME-GCN 73.8%); AD vs. NC: 84.7% (+5.1% over MME-GCN 79.6%); MCI vs. NC: 70.9% (+3.8% over Cross-GNN 67.1%). These margins are substantial and consistent across all four tasks, providing strong evidence of the method’s effectiveness. (d) The evaluation includes four metrics (ACC, SPE, SEN, AUC), more comprehensive than Papers #659 and #1496. Rich and clinically plausible interpretability analysis. Fig. 3 provides both discriminative ROI and discriminative connection analyses across all four tasks. ASD: precuneus (PCUN) and rectus gyrus (REC), consistent with social cognition and self-referential processing deficits; AD: angular gyrus (ANG) and hippocampus (HIP), reflecting memory and semantic processing impairments. The discriminative connections analysis (frontal lobe connections SFG/MFG for ASD; SFG connections for AD) adds value beyond node-level analysis and is supported by cited neuroscience literature. The ablation study (Fig. 2) effectively validates each component. Removing SGFBHE drops performance >5%; replacing SGFBHE with standard Laplacian encoding also degrades significantly, specifically validating the harmonic filtering approach over generic spectral methods; removing the Harmonic-Aware Filter consistently hurts performance. These ablation results cleanly demonstrate that performance gains stem from the proposed harmonic-specific modules rather than the Transformer backbone alone.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Core assumption limitations are not discussed. (a) Connectome harmonics assume the structural connectome is a stable substrate on which functional patterns fluctuate. In brain diseases, structural connectivity itself degenerates (e.g., white matter lesions in MS, amyloid-related disconnection in AD). Using a patient’s degraded structural connectome to define the harmonic basis may introduce systematic bias — the “Fourier basis” is itself corrupted. The paper should discuss whether harmonic modes derived from diseased structural networks remain meaningful. (b) Only the first k=40 eigenmodes are retained and high-frequency components are suppressed by the Tukey window. However, localized connectivity disruptions (e.g., focal lesions) may produce high-frequency signatures that are systematically suppressed. This design choice could miss important disease patterns. Computational complexity analysis and scalability discussion are missing. (a) Eigendecomposition (Eq. 1) is O(N³) per sample. For N=90 (AAL atlas), this is manageable, but scalability to finer parcellations (Schaefer-400, Schaefer-1000) is unclear. (b) The Harmonic-Aware Filter requires two matrix multiplications with V (N×k) per layer — GFT and IGFT. With L layers, this adds O(L·N·k·d) per sample. (c) No training/inference time comparison with baseline methods is provided. Given that several baselines (BrainGNN, BrainIB) are simpler architectures, the practical computational overhead should be quantified. Hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are incomplete. The following are set without justification or sensitivity study: (a) k=40 eigencomponents — this determines spectral resolution and is arguably the most important hyperparameter. How does performance vary for k ∈ {10, 20, 40, 60, 80}? (b) σ in Eq. (2) and Eq. (8) — controls bandwidth of radial basis filters and Gaussian smearing. (c) Tukey window parameters — controls spectral truncation behavior. (d) J=50 Gaussian basis functions — large relative to k=40 eigencomponents. (e) λ_cut = 1.1·λ_k — the cutoff frequency. These are all free parameters in the spectral filtering design, and their combined sensitivity should be analyzed. The ABIDE subset is very small (95 subjects) — the same small subset used by Paper #659.While results are strong, the 5-fold CV with ~19 test samples per fold limits generalizability claims. A cross-site generalization analysis (using ABIDE’s multi-site structure) would strengthen the paper significantly. OCREAD readout is introduced without justification for its selection over simpler alternatives (mean/sum pooling, attention pooling). The readout strategy can significantly affect graph-level classification performance, and this choice should be analyzed.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Targeted Solution to Multimodal Fusion Limitations‌: Unlike existing methods that rely on simplistic feature concatenation or treat functional and structural brain networks as independent entities, this study directly addresses the oversight of inherent structure-function coupling by leveraging connectome harmonics, providing a more biologically informed approach to multimodal brain network modeling. ‌Innovative Harmonic-Aware Modules‌: The proposed HAM-BGT framework integrates two key novel components: a Spectral Graph Filtering-Based Harmonic Encoding module that injects structural topological priors into functional connectivity representations, and a Harmonic-Aware Filter that adaptively reorganizes regional features across frequency bands. These modules enable precise extraction of harmonic-driven structure-function coupling patterns. ‌Hierarchical Dependency Capture‌: By stacking multimodal brain graph Transformer layers, HAM-BGT effectively captures local-to-global dependencies within and across brain networks, going beyond shallow fusion to model complex cross-modal interactions that are critical for accurate brain disorder diagnosis. ‌Superior Diagnostic Performance and Biomarker Discovery‌: Across multiple diagnostic tasks, HAM-BGT achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating its robustness and effectiveness. Additionally, it identifies disease-relevant biomarkers, offering actionable insights for clinical research and mechanistic studies of brain disorders. ‌Open and Reproducible Framework‌: The public availability of HAM-BGT’s implementation promotes transparency and reproducibility in the field, allowing other researchers to build on the work and further advance the understanding of structure-function coupling in brain disorders.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The experimental analysis section did not draw ROC curves, etc., to prove the reliability of the experimental results. 2.Without conducting ablation experiments, the effectiveness of the module cannot be proven. 3.Encoding only DTI data without encoding fMRI is questionable.

title: HiLoGraph: Hierarchical-Longitudinal Brain Network Representation Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated problem The idea of learning from healthy longitudinal data and using it for downstream disease detection is clinically meaningful. It avoids reliance on labels and fits well with the normative modeling literature in neuroimaging. Good combination of ideas While individual components are not new, combining multi-scale graph learning, longitudinal self-supervision, and normative modeling is interesting and works well in practice. Solid architecture + ablations The hierarchical design is sensible, and the clearly support the method. External validation Testing on an independent clinical dataset strengthens the paper.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Very small gains over strong baselines The improvements over the best baseline (LSSL) are quite small. For example, the 3-class AUC goes from 0.758 to 0.769, which is within the reported standard deviation. For AD vs LBD, performance is identical (0.731). It’s hard to tell if the added complexity provides a meaningful benefit. No statistical comparison with baselines The permutation test only shows performance above chance. There is no statistical comparison against the baselines, which seems important given how small the differences are. Limited evaluation / small clinical cohort The external dataset is relatively small (n=156, with only 20 CN), which makes the results harder to assess in terms of robustness. It would help to report variability (e. g. , across splits) or confidence intervals. Limited interpretability The model outputs deviation scores, but it is unclear which brain regions or graph components drive the predictions. Some form of regional or node-level analysis would make this more clinically useful. Clarity issues Some acronyms (e. g. , LBD) are not defined at first use. Figures are hard to interpret Fig. 2b is difficult to follow and would benefit from a clearer explanation. For Fig. 3, I do see some patterns that capture age structure for most methods. For example, why do you mention that it is not clear for fold 0 of 3HG-only?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important gap by jointly modeling: -multi-scale brain structure (ROI + fine-grained landmarks), -longitudinal dynamics This combination is novel and well justified, as prior work typically considers only one of these aspects. 2.The framework is well designed: -hierarchical GCN encoder with cross-scale fusion, -VAE latent space, -top-down decoder enforcing consistency. The design is coherent and aligns well with the problem formulation. 3.The use of temporal smoothness and contrastive constraints is a strong point. These losses explicitly enforce biologically meaningful trajectories and improve representation quality. 4.The paper includes: -multiple baselines (MLP, GCN, GAT, prior longitudinal methods), -ablations (ROI-only, 3HG-only, no longitudinal), -cross-validation. Table 1 shows consistent improvements of the full model over baselines. 5.Training only on healthy subjects and computing deviation scores is a principled and clinically relevant approach, consistent with recent literature.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.A substantial part of the analysis (e.g., Fig. 2 and Fig. 3) relies on t-SNE visualizations to support claims about: -age structure in latent space, -separation between groups. These projections are not reliable for assessing global structure or distances. While classification results are provided, the interpretability claims about the latent space are largely qualitative. 2.The evaluation dataset has only 156 subjects, class imbalance (CN = 20 vs LBD = 80). This may affect the robustness of the reported AUC values. 3.Disease prediction is performed using logistic regression on deviation features. While this isolates representation quality, it also limits performance and does not fully explore the potential of the learned embeddings. 4.The paper compares against some longitudinal baselines, but does not include stronger recent non-graph approaches (e.g., transformer-based or diffusion-based longitudinal models). This limits the positioning of the method.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper correctly identifies a genuine gap: existing longitudinal SSL methods (LSOR, LNE, LSSL) operate on volumetric data, while graph-based methods are largely cross-sectional and trained on mixed cohorts. Combining hierarchical graphs, longitudinal constraints, and pure healthy training is a reasonable and clinically meaningful contribution. 2.Following Rutherford et al. for age/sex-conditioned deviation scoring on a frozen encoder, then testing on a held-out clinical cohort, is methodologically clean and avoids label leakage. 3.The four-way comparison (ROI-only, 3HG-only, w/o longitudinal, full) is informative, and Fig. 3 nicely shows that the age manifold structure is fragile without both hierarchy and longitudinal constraints. Table 2’s feature comparison is also a good touch and supports the deviation-feature framing.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.AABC was acquired via the HCP-Aging protocol; the clinical cohort uses different scanners, sequences, and a separate preprocessing pipeline (FreeSurfer + FSL + DSI Studio vs. HCP minimal pipeline). No harmonization (e.g., ComBat, longitudinal ComBat, or a learned domain adaptation step) is reported. Apparent “deviations” in AD/LBD subjects may be partly confounded by site/scanner effects rather than true disease signal. 2.For comparison, LNE and LSSL. How were they adapted to graph inputs? Were they re-implemented from scratch? Trained on the same AABC subset with the same QC? Without these details, the baseline comparisons in Table 1 are not interpretable, and the claim that HiLoGraph beats them isn’t supportable. 3.”~400 nodes” is reported for 3HG parcellation, but 3HG extraction yields per-subject variable counts. How is the membership matrix M handled when N differs across subjects? How does the encoder handle variable-sized 3HG graphs in batches? 4.The paper produces 64-dim deviation vectors but never asks which dimensions (or which underlying ROIs/3HGs) drive the AD vs. LBD separation. Even a simple per-dimension AUC or a feature-importance plot would substantially strengthen the clinical narrative.

title: Improving Factuality of 3D Brain MRI Report Generation with Paired Image-domain Retrieval and Text-domain Augmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The work focuses on 3D MRI data, which more accurately represent the volumetric nature of neuroimaging compared to 2D slice-based methods. 2.The paper is conceptually novel in deliberately avoiding explicit image-text cross-alignment, a step that is both computationally expensive and data-intensive in existing multimodal frameworks. 3.The proposed strategy allows the model to leverage large quantities of unlabeled data via self-supervised pretraining, resulting in a strong, generalizable 3D image encoder. 4.Extensive evaluation across multiple cohorts, including external and public datasets, supports the generalizability of the approach and its potential real-world utility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.As acknowledged by the authors, PIRTA’s reliance on retrieval similarity is a major limitation. In realistic clinical contexts, rare or atypical infarct patterns may not have sufficiently similar cases in the retrieval database, leading to factual degradation and limiting clinical applicability in its current form. 2.The dataset description requires greater clarity. The appearance of “multi-class” in Figure 4 is not previously defined; it seems to refer to cases with multi-territory infarcts, but this should be explicitly stated. 3.The terms “Pretrain No,” “Small,” and “Large” used in Tables 1 and 2 are inadequately explained. The paper should quantify how many samples were used in each pretraining scale to allow reproducibility and fair interpretation. 4.The data-splitting strategy within the internal cohort is not clearly detailed. It must be explicitly stated whether train, validation, and test partitions are separated at the patient level to avoid potential overlap or retrieval leakage between training and evaluation sets. 5.The baseline comparison raises concerns of fairness. PIRTA uses full 3D volumes and retrieval-based augmentation, while the baselines operate on 2D slices without retrieval grounding. This makes the comparison only partially controlled; a 3D baseline comparison would strengthen the paper’s empirical validity.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed framework is simple but well motivated. The use of techniques such as MAE and LoRA is appropriate for the specific task. 2.The method is evaluated on multiple independent cohorts, which provides useful evidence of its robustness and potential generalizability across different data distributions.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The feature similarity used for retrieval is not sufficiently interpretable. There is a risk that the retrieval process may be driven by disease-irrelevant factors, which could reduce the reliability of reports generation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated problem formulation, highlighting the clinical importance of MRI, particularly DWI and ADC sequences, in stroke diagnosis and reporting. The proposed idea is well justified. Stroke reporting is time critical and typically follows structured patterns, making it a suitable candidate for automated report generation. The retrieval based approach is intuitive and aligns with clinical reasoning, as radiologists often rely on comparing current cases with previously seen examples. The study is supported by a large and diverse dataset, including 1,831 internal cases (993 stroke and 838 controls), as well as two external cohorts (n = 580 and n = 206, including the ISLES benchmark), which strengthens the validity and generalizability of the results. The experimental setup is well described, and the results are presented in a clear and appropriate manner. The authors conduct extensive experiments, including analysis of different levels of pretraining for the image encoder, and provide comparisons against strong baselines such as GPT 4o and LLaVA Med, demonstrating a thorough and competitive evaluation. They also acknowledge the shortcomings of current metrics such as ROUGE or BLEU in assessing clinical correctness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The definition of evaluation classes raises concerns. The categorization into normal, anterior, deep gray, posterior, and multiclass is not aligned with standard clinical frameworks such as vascular territories (for example MCA, PCA, ACA). Additionally, the manuscript does not provide a detailed explanation or justification for these classes, and it remains unclear whether hemispheric differences are taken into account. This limits the interpretability of the reported results. The discussion section is relatively limited and does not sufficiently analyze the implications of the results. In particular, the clinical quality of the generated reports is not discussed in depth. While stroke reporting is often structured (for example using ASPECTS), the current evaluation does not capture important aspects of clinical reporting and appears to rely primarily on the predefined coarse classes. A significant portion of the manuscript is dedicated to methodological and mathematical explanations, particularly Sections 2.1 (Problem Definition and Cross-modal Learning Complexity) and 2.2 (PIRTA: Paired Image-domain Retrieval and Text-domain Augmentation). While these sections are clearly written, they could be more concise to allow for a more thorough discussion of results and limitations, especially given that the primary focus of the work is report generation. Figures 2 and 4 are relatively small and visually dense, which makes them difficult to interpret.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers and respond by theme. A. Territory scheme (R3.W1, R1.W2). The four-class scheme is a coarse vascular-territory label set consistent with AHA/ASA stroke imaging guidelines [Powers, Stroke, 2019]. It is not a per-vessel ontology. Anterior maps to ACA/MCA cortical territories, deep gray to lenticulostriate (MCA-deep), posterior to PCA/vertebrobasilar, and normal to no infarct. This grouping preserves class support while retaining clinically actionable localization. Finer ASPECTS/per-vessel evaluation is future work (R3.W2). B. Data integrity and pretraining quantification (R1.W3, R1.W4). Train/validation/test are split strictly at the patient level. No patient appears in multiple splits, and the retrieval database is built from training-set embeddings only, so validation/test images never serve as retrieval candidates (to be stated in Sec. 3). “Pretrain Large” = MAE on 38,532 UK Biobank subjects (Sec. 3.1), “Small” = MAE on the internal cohort only (~1,831), and “No” = random initialization. Counts will be added to the table caption. C. Baseline fairness (R1.W5). GPT-4o and LLaVA-Med are 2D image-conditioned models with no public 3D variant; we fed them the lesion-centered axial slice (mid-brain if unavailable) and identical prompts (Sec. 4.2). To address medical-domain specificity, we additionally evaluated Med-Gemma (a medical-domain VLM) under both slice strategies. Multi-class territory accuracy on internal/BRMH/ISLES: PIRTA 89.9/71.4/67.0; Med-Gemma v1 lesion 17.5/20.2/11.2, middle 24.4/21.4/18.4; v1.5 lesion 31.3/36.4/22.3, middle 32.7/36.9/21.8; best general-purpose VLM 29.4/21.7/36.4.Across all 2D baselines, PIRTA leads by at least +57.2/+34.5/+30.6 points (best 2D = Med-Gemma v1.5 on internal/BRMH, GPT-4o on ISLES). Per-class gap persists (posterior 95.4 vs <=34.8 internal, 87.4 vs <=50.6 BRMH). A 3D-supervised medical baseline remains the next step. D. Retrieval interpretability and rare-case reliance (R2.W1, R1.W1). The retrieval encoder is supervised for ischemic-territory classification. Its embedding space reaches 94.04 / 71.21 / 70.87 mAP@1 (Table 1) and 93.06 / 69.23 / 68.10% multi-class territory accuracy (Table 2) on internal / BRMH / ISLES, indicating disease-relevant feature encoding rather than generic image similarity. Cosine similarity is a confidence cue. In Sec. 4.2, high-similarity retrievals align with correct territory generation, while low-similarity rare patterns mark cases needing clinical review. We agree this is a real limitation. We will make it explicit and treat hybrid retrieval with multimodal evidence as the next step. E. Discussion depth (R3.W2). We adopted ischemic-territory accuracy because n-gram metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) miss clinically important errors, whereas territory is a clinically actionable report attribute for stroke localization and reperfusion triage (Sec. 4.2). The Discussion will be expanded to (i) clarify clinical implications of retrieval-grounded factuality, (ii) frame territory accuracy as a focused factuality surrogate rather than a complete report-quality metric, and (iii) delineate ASPECTS-style scoring and prospective expert evaluation as planned axes. F. Specifics. (R1.W2) “Multi-class” in Fig. 4 means multi-territory infarcts (>=2 territories), which the caption will define. (R3.W3) Sec. 2.1-2.2 will be tightened to free space for the expanded Discussion. (R3.W4) Fig. 2 and Fig. 4 will be enlarged within page limits. (R3) Hemispheric distinction is not in the current label set and is left for per-vessel work. Pretraining scale matters. Tables 1-2 show +13.3/+14.5/+32.0 mAP@1 and +11.1/+16.1/+28.1 multi-class points (Large vs No) on internal/BRMH/ISLES, supporting large-scale SSL for cross-institution generalization. G. Reproducibility (R1.7, R2.7). If accepted, we will release source code (training, inference, baselines, evaluation).

title: Interpretable Structure-Function Coupling via State-Space Models for Brain Connectome Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: [1]. The proposed Hierarchical Fusion Variant (GM-SSFuse-H) model is novel. The proposed framework (GM-SSFuse) consists of modality-specific Graph Mamba (GM) encoders and a hierarchical variant (GM-SSFuse-H) based on the prior of the modular organization of the brain. [2]. Graph Mamba (GM) Encoder: Graph-augmented input concatenating node features information and a one-hop neighborhood aggregattion) and Topology-aware node ordering evaluated by degree, breadth-first search, depth-first search and spectral analysis. [3]. The GM-SSFuse-H operates at two levels: within-module fusion and cross-module integration. [4]. This study defines three quantitative interaction metrics: active pair fraction, mean hop distance, and cross-module ratio, to validate distributed SC-FC coupling. [5]. The workload for data analysis is substantial. The constructed model has undergone a comprehensive evaluation, with its effectiveness validated on four datasets and compared with multiple methods. Additionally, ablation and qualitative analysis have also been conducted.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: For each disease classification, the number of participants for both disease and control groups is relatively small in this study: PPMI (75 controls, 72 PD patients), ADNI (105 controls, 100 AD patients), and COBRE (72 controls, 60 SZ patients). For the comparison of results from different methods, it is recommended to provide the results of statistical tests.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Previous studies on SC-FC coupling either use Pearson (or Spearman) correlation on one-to-one paired coupling. Some new methods use learning-based algorithms to generate FC from SC or vice versa. This paper follows similar direction by measuring nonlinear, complex (many-to-many) SC-FC coupling. The advantage is that it uses hidden state propagation to allow influence across all regions without explicitly enumerating O(N²) pairs. 2.The proposed hierarchical modular fusion (GM-SSFuse-H) takes biologically informative principles (modular structure) into SC-FC coupling by conducting within-module Mamba followed by a second Mamba, respecting the brain’s modular organization. 3.Quantitative interaction metrics: Proposes three novel metrics (active pair fraction, mean hop distance, cross-module ratio) derived from learned weights to validate distributed coupling empirically with extended interpretability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Why does a region j in fMRI have to be subsequent to region i in structural connectivity? The interleaved ordering creates a sequential chain that is convenient for Mamba, but it is not biologically meaningful because no brain region in either fMRI or DTI studies inherently possesses such sequential information. That is, region i does not necessarily precede region j in any anatomical or functional sense. Although the authors acknowledge this issue by stating that “The Mamba hidden state at position t accumulates information from all preceding positions, so the order in which nodes are presented to the scan determines which neighborhood relationships are captured implicitly through state propagation,” the imposed ordering can still introduce a significant violation of neurobiological plausibility. Moreover, whether the order is determined by data‑driven or hypothesis‑driven means, it may carry biased information. If the ordering is permuted, the results could be entirely different. The authors ultimately report that “BFS is optimal for FC and degree ordering for SC, and use these throughout,” which indeed indicates that the ordering itself is a sensitive parameter. 2.Did the authors compare their method with conventional Spearman correlation‑based SC‑FC coupling approaches? How does the correlation coefficient r obtained from the proposed method compare to that from these traditional methods? – it seems that the current method cannot explicitly output such an r. 3.How are the modules defined? Is the modular partition data‑specific? Does the module detection procedure introduce bias? 4.The idea of first integrating information within modules and then across different modules lacks a clear biological substrate. The existence of direct connections between regions belonging to different modules or communities is beyond question. 5.What is the biological meaning or interpretability behind such an end‑to‑end model that directly outputs a diagnostic label or a regression score? 6.The four datasets appear to have been used to train separate models, each trained from scratch. Could different datasets be combined to train a joint model (e.g., with additional fine‑tuning layers for different tasks)?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Utilizing interleaved sequences in a Mamba-based state-space model to achieve this without explicitly computing 𝑂(𝑁2) pairs is an elegant and highly novel methodological contribution to the field of connectomics. 2.The introduction of the hierarchical variant (GM-SSFuse-H) demonstrates a strong understanding of brain topology. The experimental setup is robust. Testing the framework across four diverse datasets encompassing both regression (fluid cognition) and classification (PD, AD, SZ) strongly validates the generalizability of the proposed method. 4.The introduction of specific metrics to quantify the distributed nature of the coupling is a major strength. The gradient-based attribution analysis and the resulting circular connectome plots provide compelling qualitative evidence that aligns with known disease pathologies.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While Section 2.2 mentions that four node orderings were evaluated (and BFS/degree were found optimal), the quantitative results of this comparison are missing. Please provide a supplementary table detailing the performance variance across the different traversal strategies (BFS, DFS, Degree, Spectral, and perhaps Random). This will help the community understand the robustness of SSMs on graph data. 2.In Figure 3 (top), the “Cross-Attn” ablation is shown. Could you clarify in the text exactly how this cross-attention was formulated? Does it compute dense N×N attention between SC and FC nodes?
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback. We address the key concerns below. Node ordering and biological plausibility (R2.W1, R3.W1): We evaluated the four orderings on PPMI. Performance across BFS, DFS, and Degree is stable, with BFS marginally optimal for FC and Degree for SC. As MICCAI does not permit PDF supplementary materials, we were unable to include these ablations in the submission. We will publish full ablations on node ordering as supplementary material upon publication. The interleaved ordering is not claimed to be biologically sequential in the sense that region i anatomically precedes region j. The ordering determines which neighbourhood relationships are captured implicitly through hidden state propagation. BFS groups topologically proximal FC nodes consecutively, encouraging local neighbourhood coherence; degree ordering for SC places hub regions early, maximising early-state coverage. Comparison with Spearman/Pearson SC-FC coupling (R2.W2): Traditional couplings produce a scalar coupling coefficient per subject by correlating SC and FC edge weights across region pairs. Our framework operates in a different paradigm: it is discriminative and end-to-end, using SC-FC coupling as a learned feature for downstream prediction rather than as a standalone biomarker. The interaction metrics serve as our characterisation of coupling breadth, analogous to but not directly comparable with classical coupling coefficients. Modular fusion biological justification (R2.W4): We agree that direct cross-module structural connections exist; this is precisely why GM-SSFuse-H does not hard-block inter-module interactions. The within-module stage provides a biologically informed inductive bias constraining early fusion to functionally coherent groups. The cross-module Mamba scan in the second stage explicitly accommodates inter-network interactions. As discussed in Section 3, the flat variant is particularly effective for schizophrenia where dysconnectivity is globally distributed and does not respect module boundaries, which further supports this design choice. Module definition (R2.W3): The partition is the modified Yeo 7-network parcellation with an added subcortical module (P=8), as stated in Section 2.1.It is atlas-derived, fixed across all subjects and datasets, and not learned from data, introducing no data-dependent bias. Cross-dataset training (R2.W6): Joint training across datasets is non-trivial given the different label spaces (regression vs. three distinct disease classifications) and heterogeneous acquisition protocols; separate models follow the same convention as all compared baselines. Corrections made in the camera-ready Section 2.1: Key preprocessing steps added. fMRI images were preprocessed with fMRIPrep, including motion correction, slice timing correction, spatial normalisation to MNI152NLin2009cAsym space, and nuisance regression. DTI images were preprocessed via Clinica and FSL, including eddy current correction and probabilistic tractography; SC matrix entries are streamline counts between ROI pairs following the AAL atlas (R1, comments 1 and 2). Section 2.3, Formula 4: Fully connected layer notation renamed from FC1/FC2 to Lin1/Lin2 to avoid confusion with the functional connectivity abbreviation FC (R1, comment 3). Section 3, Ablation: Cross-attention baseline clarified as scaled dot-product attention between SC node embeddings as queries and FC node embeddings as keys and values, producing a dense N x N interaction map (R3, comment 2). We note that specificity metrics (R1, comment 4), statistical tests, the full node ordering ablation, encoder ablation, effect of pretraining, and further SC-FC coupling weight matrix analysis could not be included due to page constraints. These will be published as supplementary material upon publication.
