title: Joint Multi-modal Learning for Susceptibility-Induced Distortion Correction in Diffusion MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The method is technically sound. Introducing FOD into distortion correction is a natural yet powerful design. 2.Evaluations include multiple datasets with well-designed metrics. I like the fact that the authors paid special attention to important brain structures that are interesting to neuroscientists but susceptible to distortions. 3.The paper is well-written, and figures are scientifically decent.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Several technical details warrant clearer justifications and clarifications: 1.The integration of FOD image is helpful for distortion correction, but it also introduces another layer of complexity. Specifically: (1) Does this add requirement for the number of diffusion directions of the dataset to give robust FOD estimation? How would the method perform on data with limited directions (e. g. , 6 for DTI fitting that is common in clinical practice). (2) The original workflow for dMRI preprocessing is: topup using b=0 -> eddy correction -> downstream analyses; in the paper, what the authors proposed is: eddy for one PE -> FOD fitting -> eddy for another PE -> FOD fitting -> distortion correction using proposed MMDC-Net -> eddy for the entire dataset -> downstream analyses. This looks rather complicated. It is worth quantifying or at least discussing this additional burden. 2.Without FOD, the loss function is essentially very similar to FSL TOPUP using only b=0 as input but with a neural network optimization. However, looking at the results, b=0 only MMDC-Net is consistently outperformed by TOPUP. It’s worth finding out why.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The overall motivation is reasonable. Combining B0 and FOD information for distortion correction is a natural idea. In brain dMRI distortion correction, B0 information can be insufficient in certain regions such as the brainstem, whereas FOD may provide additional structural guidance. This motivation is not arbitrary and is well connected to prior work in this area, including FODReg (2019), which used FOD to estimate the distortion field in brainstem connectome imaging, and DrC-Net (2022), which further developed FOD-based correction in a deep learning framework. Another strength is that the method is fairly comprehensive in design. The proposed FDM module attempts to combine both B0 and FOD information, and the use of PCGrad is also a reasonable design choice in a multi-objective setting. In addition, the paper includes extensive comparisons and ablation studies, which help support the empirical evaluation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: A major concern is that much of the novelty appears to be compositional. The method mainly integrates several existing ingredients, such as FOD-based supervision, Jacobian-style intensity modulation, and PCGrad, rather than introducing a fundamentally new principle for distortion correction. Related to this, based on the paper’s description, the FDM module generates a two-channel attention map to perform spatially adaptive reweighting of B0 and FOD features. This seems closer to a modality weighting or attention-gating mechanism. In that sense, describing it as “feature disentanglement” feels somewhat overstated. Another issue is the scope implied by the title. The title suggests a more general framework for diffusion MRI distortion correction, but all experiments are conducted on brain datasets, and the second modality used here, FOD, is itself highly brain-specific. As a result, the empirical scope appears narrower than the title suggests.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Paper is well written and motivation is clear and the method well explained. Each of the components of the proposed method seems sensible and well-motivated. The proposed method shows good performance compared to the reference methods, outperforming the widely used standard topup and other comparator DL methods. Method shows good generalisability onto unseen data with same phase-encoding direction, comparable to existing DL SoA. Ablation study is nice to demonstrate the benefit of each of the components.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main thought is around the use of the FOD in the uncorrected images and whether that is fundamentally sound. As I understand it, susceptibility distortions mean that signal that “should” be in certain voxels get accumulated or spread into other voxels which would mean that the FOD you estimate in those distorted voxels is wrong. Then, simply spatially transforming the SH coefficients with the estimated distortion field would not result in the correct FOD being reconstructed. So I think the blip up and blip down “corrected” FODs will not be the same even if the distortion could be perfectly corrected. I think this why FODreg and DrC-Net first use topup+eddy, to get initial FODs that are already close to correct and the FOD step is more of a refinement. That said, it seems that the FOD method may be “good enough” since it seems to help. Figure 3 is quite small and requires a lot of zooming in to parse. What do the asterisks mean in Table 2? In Section 3.1, HCP, HCP-Aging and HCLV acronyms are introduced without definition
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments. Reviewer#1 1.Does incorporating FOD add requirements for the number of diffusion directions? How would the method perform on data with limited directions? FOD estimation requires sufficient directions; fewer directions degrade reconstruction precision and correction performance. To address this, integrating deep learning to estimate robust FODs from limited-direction data represents a valuable future direction. 2.The proposed preprocessing workflow is complicated. What is the additional computational burden? While prior eddy current correction and FOD reconstruction requires extra computation compared to B0-based methods, this is a necessary step for all FOD-based methods. Fast deep learning tools for these steps now greatly reduce this burden. We will discuss this computational trade-off in the discussion of the revision. 3.Why is the b=0 only MMDC-Net consistently outperformed by FSL TOPUP? TOPUP uses iterative optimization with a multi-resolution pyramid, achieving excellent instance alignment at the cost of extremely long running times. Conversely, our B0-only baseline is a single forward-pass network lacking iterative multi-scale refinement, explaining the performance gap. Reviewer#2 1.The novelty appears compositional, and the term “feature disentanglement” is overstated. Our primary contribution lies in the joint multi-modal modeling of the susceptibility-induced distortion correction issue and the specific modules designed to resolve modality conflicts. We agree the term may be overstated. To accurately reflect its function of recalibrating regional feature contributions, we will rename FDM to the “Modality-Aware Attention Module” in the revision. 2.The title implies a broader scope, but the method and experiments are highly brain-specific. Susceptibility-induced distortions are severe in the brain (e.g., near brainstem/orbitofrontal tissue-air boundaries) and critically impact downstream connectome analyses. Most existing susceptibility distortion correction works are exclusively validated on brain datasets. Future work will extend our framework to other anatomies, such as the spine, to comprehensively evaluate its generalizability. 3.Does the FOD branch truly not require Jacobian-based intensity correction? As visually evident in our data, the intensity bias (signal pile-up or loss) observed in raw images like B0 does not manifest in the corresponding regions of the FOD images. As shown in the comparison of the same spatial location in Fig.1(c), the FOD exhibit no intensity distortion compared to B0.4.Are the components in the ablation study (Table 2) added independently or cumulatively? They are added cumulatively. We will update the Table 2 caption to state: “Components are added cumulatively to the baseline.” 5.Does the method improve high-b DWI or other diffusion metrics beyond FOD? The estimated deformation field is applied to all raw images. Our evaluation already uses Fractional Anisotropy (FA)—a tensor-derived metric calculated from corrected diffusion images. The improved FA MSD scores (Tab.1, Fig. 2) explicitly prove our method successfully corrects raw DWIs and enhances downstream diffusion metrics beyond FODs. Reviewer#4 1.Is computing and transforming FODs directly on uncorrected, distorted images fundamentally sound? This is valid and widely accepted. Because local diffusion characteristics are consistent, raw DWIs and B0 images share the identical spatial distortion. And the voxel-wise FOD estimation introduces no extra deformation. Consequently, the uncorrected FODs preserve the original distortion and can be used to estimate the deformation field. 2.Fig.3 is too small. What do the ‘ ’ mean in Tab.2? Acronyms in Sec 3.1 are undefined. We will correct these by: 1) enlarging Fig. 3 to show key results; 2) clarifying in Tab.2 that ‘ ’ denotes baselines lacking proposed modules; 3) defining all dataset acronyms (HCP, HCP-Aging, HCLV) in Sec. 3.1.

title: PRISM: Differentiable Analysis-by-Synthesis for Fixel Recovery in Diffusion MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) This reviewer found the methodology novel, ambitious and well motivated. Particularly the integration of components typically considered “pre-processing” directly into the microstructure inverse problem is a good direction. 2) The quantitative results are promising in comparison to standard techniques, if not state of the art techniques at this point (see item 3 on weaknesses).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) A key component of the method is spatial regularization. Particularly, the authors mention several priors used to regularize the peaks, including a “direction continuity”. What is this penalty function? How it handle/associate multiple peaks? More explanation would be helpful. 2) How are the prior regularizer penalties (the lambdas) set? Presumably, these will depend on acquisition parameters and SNR. Can the authors provide guidance on how to tune/set them in practice for different datasets. How sensitive is the method to their values? 3) There are a variety of recent (deep) learning-based approaches to FOD estimation which have reported to largely surpass the performance over CSD family of methods (see Section 4.5 of [1] for a non exhaustive list). The numerical experiments would be improved by comparing with one (or several) representative examples from this class of methods. 4) The method fixes the diffusivities. This can lead to bias in peak identification when microstructure differs significantly from nominal values [2]. This should at least be acknowledged, and ideally evaluated via simulation. 5) Some visual comparison of the recovered FOD fields between the methods would be a very helpful supplement to the quantitative results for evaluation. [1] Davood Karimi, Simon K. Warfield; Diffusion MRI with machine learning. Imaging Neuroscience 2024. [2] Guo F, et. al. Fiber orientation distribution from diffusion MRI: Effects of inaccurate response function calibration. J Neuroimaging. 2021.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The end-to-end joint optimization of tissue parameters together with nuisance calibration (bias field, per-measurement affine, noise level) is a clean and to my knowledge novel reformulation of a pipeline that is typically split into separate preprocessing and fitting stages. The Rician NLL formulation with self-supervised sigma recovery is a useful addition and produces a meaningful improvement over MSE. The crossing-fiber benchmark is designed to be in the author’s disfavor: PRISM uses a deliberately mismatched D_perp (0.4 versus the true 0.3), while CSD and MSMT-CSD receive oracle response functions. Outperforming oracle-initialized baselines under this setup is a strong result. The related work section is quite thorough and detailed to my knowledge and correctly situates PRISM against voxelwise classical fitters, learning-based voxelwise mappings, mesh-based differentiable simulators, and dictionary approaches. Evaluation is quite through since it spans synthetic, phantom, and in-vivo data with multiple metrics.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The forward model and the source of differentiability are not clearly specified. Equations 3-5 define a closed-form analytic signal, so “differentiability” here appears to mean standard autodiff over analytic compartments rather than a custom differentiable solver. The term “differentiable” often implies a custom solver in related work, so stating explicitly that the forward model is closed-form with gradients from autodiff (and naming the framework such as PyTorch, Julia or JAX) would resolve the ambiguity and distinguish the contribution from differentiable simulator-based methods. The DiSCo1 ablation shows the restricted compartment drops r by 9.4 pp when removed, versus 1.9 pp for topology and 0.7 pp for spatial priors. Without the restricted compartment PRISM scores r = 0.840, below MSMT-CSD at 0.920.Since the baselines do not include this compartment, part of the headline gain is model capacity, not the analysis-by-synthesis framework. Either give MSMT-CSD an equivalent compartment or report PRISM without the restricted compartment alongside baselines. No sensitivity analysis for regularization. The method uses at least six tissue regularizers (spatial smoothness, direction repulsion, sparsity, orphan-WM, directional continuity, fiber ordering) plus calibration L2 and Total Variation, all with fixed global weights. It is not clear which are load-bearing, and the calibration regularizer weights and the 8^3 bias-field grid size are not justified or discussed. No qualitative results. Only quantitative metrics are reported. Visualizations of fiber orientations, ODFs, or tractography on the phantom or HCP against baselines would support the numbers better and show failure modes. The “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” framing somewhat overclaims. In practice this is gradient-based fitting of an analytic multi-compartment model with joint nuisance estimation, which is close to what the NODDI or SANDI toolbox already do. Comparing against those methods, not only simulator-based ones, would make the actual difference (joint nuisance calibration, Rician NLL with learned sigma, patch-based spatial regularization) clearer.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The novelty of this paper mainly resides in the optimisation of the nuisance calibration parameters simultaneously to the microstructure parameters, correcting for nuisances that may survive preprocessing. The forward model includes many compartments (CSF, gray matter, up to K white matter fiber compartments and a restricted compartment), which enables to capture many different microstructural environments. Experiments to evaluate the benefits of the calibration module are performed, showing it reduces angular error in the presence of intensity nuisance factors, but also that it does not affect microstructure parameter estimation in unperturbed data.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: PRISM performs global rather than voxel-wise optimisation, but its performance is compared solely against voxel-wise methods. A comparison with other global optimisation algorithms should be made. (e.g. Daducci A, Dal Palù A, Lemkaddem A, Thiran JP. COMMIT: Convex optimization modeling for microstructure informed tractography. IEEE Trans Med Imaging. 2015 Jan;34(1):246-57.doi: 10.1109/TMI.2014.2352414.) Furthermore, spatial information via regularisation has previously been employed, but no comparisons have been made. (e.g. A. Ramirez-Manzanares, M. Rivera, B. C. Vemuri, P. Carney and T. Mareci, “Diffusion Basis Functions Decomposition for Estimating White Matter Intravoxel Fiber Geometry,” in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 26, no. 8, pp. 1091-1102, Aug. 2007, doi: 10.1109/TMI.2007.900461.) Qualitative results are not presented, impeding visual verification of the reported improvements to fiber recovery. No comparisons to other methods are made for the real data experiment.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and area chair for their constructive feedback. 1.Differentiability and positioning (R2, meta). The forward model (Eqs. 2-5) is a closed-form analytic multi-compartment expression; “differentiable” refers to gradient propagation via PyTorch autograd, not a custom solver, distinguishing PRISM from FEM-based simulators. In contrast to voxelwise fitters (CSD, NODDI, SANDI), PRISM jointly estimates bias field, per-measurement affine correction and noise level with microstructure; optimises 3-D slabs with neighbour-aware regularisation; and supports Rician NLL with self-supervised sigma. 2.Direction-continuity penalty (R1, meta). The summed term is K-permutation-invariant and avoids explicit cross-voxel peak matching: for each fiber k we sample its own fraction along its own direction and penalise along-fiber changes, L_dc = (1/K) sum_k E_x f_k(x) (|f_k(x) - f_k(x + e d_k(x))| + |f_k(x) - f_k(x - e d_k(x))|), with e=0.5 voxel and trilinear interpolation. The f_k weighting localises the penalty to voxels carrying that fiber; +/- handles antipodal symmetry. This formula will replace the vague description. Thank you for pointing this out. 3.Restricted-compartment (R2, meta). R2 is right that part of the DiSCo1 gain reflects model capacity. Sec. 4 ablation reports PRISM without the restricted compartment at r=0.840 (full 0.934), below MSMT-CSD (0.920). PRISM’s contribution is enabling this compartment with nuisance calibration in one optimisation; we will temper Sec. 4/Discussion. 4.Fixed diffusivities (R1). Kernel diffusivities are fixed by design, following NODDI/SANDI/MSMT-CSD practice: joint estimation of diffusivities, fractions and directions is ill-conditioned at clinical SNR/shell counts (Jelescu 2016). PRISM still learns per voxel S_0, all K+3 fractions, K fiber directions and f_intra (Sec. 2). The synthetic benchmark probes this: PRISM uses D_perp=0.4 (Eq. 5) while baselines receive oracle/ground-truth-derived response functions (Sec. 3); despite this mismatch PRISM achieves 1.9x lower angular error at SNR=30 (Table 1). We will acknowledge in the revised version that a larger mismatch can bias peaks. 5.Missing comparisons (R1, R3, meta). (a) Many learning-based FOD methods (Karimi & Warfield 2024) need labelled training/protocol matching; PRISM is training-free. (b) COMMIT (Daducci 2015) weights streamlines from a precomputed tractogram, complementary to local FOD/fixel recovery. (c) DBF (Ramirez-Manzanares 2007) is relevant prior work on intra-voxel basis-function FOD; differs in scope from PRISM’s multi-compartment setting. (d) NODDI/SANDI are voxelwise analytic fitters, not K-crossing FOD baselines. Positioning will be revised. 6.Regularisation sensitivity (R1, R2, meta). Because signals are b0-normalised, all tissue weights are fixed when enabled (lambda_sp = lambda_rep = 0.01, lambda_sparse = 0.02; orphan/order = 0.01, dc = 0.005; Sec. 2), with no per-dataset tuning. Per Sec. 3, synthetic uses repulsion only, DiSCo1 adds topology, HCP the full suite; weights do not change. Sec. 4 ablation isolates each block: spatial 0.7 pp, topology 1.9 pp, restricted 9.4 pp. Calibration weights and the 8^3 bias-field grid were also fixed; the grid limits bias to low spatial frequencies. A systematic sweep is future work. 7.Qualitative figures and HCP scope (all reviewers, R3). HCP lacks ground-truth fiber orientations, so it is not claimed as a ground-truth fiber benchmark; head-to-head comparisons use synthetic and DiSCo1 data because they provide ground truth. If accepted, the camera-ready will add fiber-peak overlays from existing fits, within the additional page. 8.Eq. 9 typo (R3). The -log y term was dropped in transcription; it is a data-only constant independent of all optimised parameters, so gradients, fits and reported numbers are unaffected. We will correct it. We commit to releasing source code upon acceptance. Thank you again for these thoughtful suggestions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): All three reviewers recognize the clear motivation, the novel joint nuisance-calibration framework, and the promising quantitative results of the proposed PRISM method, yet persistent critical concerns place the paper near the acceptance threshold. The authors must prioritize addressing these core points in their rebuttal. 1) Clarify the concrete formulation of spatial regularizers (especially direction continuity penalty) and provide sensitivity analysis plus practical tuning guidance for regularization weights; 2) Reframe the claimed “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” contribution to avoid overstatement and clarify technical distinctions from prior arts; 3) Extend experimental comparisons with learning-based FOD estimation methods, global optimization baselines, and classic analytical models like NODDI; 4) Justify fixed diffusivity settings, explain unbalanced multi-compartment designs against baseline methods, and specify the implementation of differentiable optimization. | After careful review of the initial assessments, the author’s rebuttal, and post-rebuttal responses, I recommend rejecting this paper for several reasons. The primary concern is the lack of sensitivity analysis for the numerous regularization parameters, raising doubts about the method’s applicability to new datasets with varying characteristics. The authors’ claim that weights are fixed globally is problematic, as it does not provide guidance for practitioners. Additionally, the paper fails to compare PRISM with relevant state-of-the-art learning-based FOD estimation techniques, which are vital for contextualizing its performance. The absence of qualitative results also hinders the assessment of the recovered fiber orientations. Although reviewers expressed willingness to accept based on proposed changes, acceptance should rely solely on the current manuscript, which lacks essential components for a complete scientific contribution. The reviewer, confident in their assessment, maintained a Reject recommendation, highlighting substantive concerns about hyperparameter sensitivity and incomplete evaluations. The framing of “differentiable analysis-by-synthesis” remains overstated; the method is more of a gradient-based fitting approach similar to existing models like NODDI and SANDI. While the joint nuisance calibration is a valuable contribution, it does not represent a significant paradigm shift in the field. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers are generally positive after rebuttal, with two recommending acceptance and one maintaining a borderline rejection. The remaining concerns mainly relate to clearer reporting of differentiability, hyperparameter sensitivity, qualitative examples, and acknowledging the restricted-compartment capacity effect. Since these issues appear addressable in the camera-ready rather than fatal to the contribution, I recommend Accept. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Even though reviewer 1 is not wrong in suggesting that this paper would benefit from a larger revision, assuming that all the changes that have been promised in the rebuttal will be made to the final version, and code will be released, the paper is clearly among the stronger ones in my rebuttal batch already. Some of the suggested additional experiments might not fit within the MICCAI page limit anyway, and might thus be left for future work.

title: Spinverse: Differentiable Physics for Permeability-Aware Microstructure Reconstruction from Diffusion MRI
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper introduces a fully differentiable Bloch-Torrey simulator integrated into an inverse-design pipeline. This approach embeds the fundamental physics of diffusion MRI directly into the optimization loop. The method successfully unifies topological freedom with biophysical realism. By parameterizing boundaries as continuous face permeabilities, it not only allows complex, non-predefined shapes to emerge (topology-free), but also explicitly models semi-permeable water exchange—a critical physiological factor often ignored by traditional compartmental models. 3.The paper demonstrates a sophisticated staged optimization strategy. The authors provide a robust solution to the local minima problem inherent in complex inverse physics problems.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The iterative optimization process is computationally expensive, taking approximately 33 minutes per voxel on a single 24GB NVIDIA L4 GPU GPU. Thus the method faces severe scalability issues when attempting to reconstruct higher-resolution grids or larger volumes, making it currently impractical for whole-brain or even small-ROI clinical applications. 2.Despite the proposed curriculum learning strategy, the inverse problem remains highly non-convex. The reconstruction quality is heavily dependent on the specific choice of b-values and diffusion times. 3.The evaluation is exclusively performed on noise-free or low-noise synthetic data. Clinical dMRI is frequently corrupted by Rician noise, eddy current distortions, and motion artifacts. It is unclear how the emergent permeability field would behave under realistic SNR conditions, where noise could be misinterpreted as phantom boundaries.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel topology-free boundary representation. 2.End-to-end differentiable pipeline. 3.Stronger boundary validity than learned baselines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Evaluation scope is very limited. 2.Scalability and computational cost are prohibitive. 3.Multi-compartment performance is poor without clear diagnosis. 4.Threshold τ_b is not robustly validated. 5.Missing implementation details (The paper does not specify how many tetrahedra the ambient mesh contains, what the mesh resolution is relative to the ground-truth geometry, or how many eigenmodes are retained in the truncated eigendecomposition.) 6.compare against non-differentiable physics-based microstructure inversion approaches (e.g., ActiveAx, CHARMED) or recent learned inverse problem solvers (unrolled networks, deep equilibrium models) that could serve as alternative baselines for the inverse problem formulation
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) This reviewer appreciates the novelty and ambition of the work. To my knowledge, this is a novel, rich parameteterization of the microstructure and this work lays the ground work of an inversion scheme that can be subsequently built upon. 2) The experiments, while simple and only use simulated data, are comprehensive, demonstrate the potential of the method and clearly highlight the effect of key methodological components, e.g. multi-stage optimization, priors, etc. 3) Authors explicitly identify configurations the method struggles in (multi-compartment), which is both refreshing and helps promote subsequent research.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) This reviewer is skeptical on the statistical identifiability of model parameters (the kappas) in practical diffusion acqusitions with realistic noise levels. Perhaps some between voxel spatial regularzation could help here (extending priors to adjacent faces in neighboring voxels?). In any case, this is beyond the scope of the current work, but could be investigated in the journal version. 2) Related to 1, ways to select prior regularization strength hyperparameters will be needed for practical adoption, but again this is well beyond the scope.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their careful reading and constructive feedback. We are pleased that the novelty of the topology-free permeability parameterization and differentiable Bloch-Torrey pipeline is recognized across all reviews, and address the major concerns below. [Noise Robustness (R1, R2)] Noise sensitivity analysis is an important validation direction we acknowledge. With space constraints in the submission, we chose to focus on establishing the theoretical framework and its viability against learned baselines. Regarding eddy currents and motion, these are preprocessing-level corruptions handled prior to microstructure estimation by standard pipelines (NODDI/SANDI). Comprehensive noise characterization is central to the planned journal extension. [Baseline Comparisons - ActiveAx and CHARMED (R2)] ActiveAx/CHARMED are parametric compartment models in the same category as NODDI/SANDI, which we already discuss in the paper as representative of this class. They produce no explicit boundary reconstruction; a Chamfer distance comparison is undefined for methods that output no surface. Our learned baselines (MLP, GNN) are the natural alternatives, they operate on the same tetrahedral mesh and output face permeabilities directly. Unrolled networks and deep equilibrium models are valid for inverse imaging problems broadly, but adapting them to mesh-based boundary reconstruction is non-trivial and constitutes additional work outside the scope of the paper. [Multi-Compartment Failure Diagnosis (R2)] The multi-compartment results provide an honest representation of where the method succeeds (single-axon) and where it struggles (two-axon, multi-compartment). We explicitly acknowledge in our paper that multi-compartment optimization remains an open problem. The paper identifies multiple candidate explanations: (i) rotational degeneracy collapses reconstructions toward symmetric envelopes, (ii) inferring multiple interfaces from the same acquisition is inherently more ill-posed, and (iii) single-compartment regularization strengths may collapse multi-compartment boundaries. We are actively pursuing solutions to this problem. [Missing Implementation Details (R2)] These details were omitted from Sec 4.The reconstruction and reference share the same ambient mesh (576 tetrahedra, 189 vertices, 1296 faces); they differ only in permeability values assigned to faces, so mesh resolution is identical by construction. The truncated eigendecomposition retains 500 eigenmodes per mesh. These will be added to the Setup paragraph. [Computational Cost (R1, R2)] We acknowledge that 33 minutes per voxel is a current limitation of the approach. Physics-based inversion requires a full PDE solve per optimization iteration, inherently more expensive than parametric methods. Unlike learned methods, Spinverse requires no training data and generalizes across acquisition protocols and mesh resolutions without retraining; a flexibility that comes at inference-time cost. Accelerating physics-based microstructure solvers is an active area of our research, including hybrid learning-based initialization and optimized eigensolvers to reduce spectral decomposition cost. [Threshold Analysis (R2)] Tau_b=10^-3 is the log-space midpoint of the optimized permeability range [10^-5, 10^-1], which was determined empirically from forward model experiments. The threshold was further informed by the distribution of optimized face permeabilities at convergence, where boundary faces consistently fall below this value. [Non-Convexity and Acquisition Sensitivity (R1)] Regarding acquisition sensitivity, non-convexity is mitigated but not eliminated by the staged curriculum(Fig3), which avoids gradient-conflict failure modes of joint optimization, and the regularizers(Eq3) constrain the search to physically plausible fields. Achievable accuracy is fundamentally bounded by signal information content, which is inherent to dMRI inverse problems and not specific to Spinverse.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Spatiotemporal Graph Learning for Individualized Cortical Parcellation and Somato-Cognitive Integration in the Developing Brain
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The framework combines multi-head local self-attention with spatial-temporal graph convolutional networks, and is applied to fMRI data to achieve individualized cortical parcellation and identify integration zones (2) The dual-channel signal (raw signal + attention-weighted neighborhood signal) preserves both local dynamics and context-modulated information (3) Probabilistic output + entropy computation：The entropy-based aggregation of high-uncertainty vertices interprets high-entropy vertices as “group-level functional integration zones”
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) Lack of comparison with other individualized parcellation methods, such as: Wang, D. , Buckner, R. , Fox, M. et al. Parcellating cortical functional networks in individuals. Nat Neurosci 18, 1853–1860 (2015). (2) Lack of ablation study: In the proposed framework, the individual contributions of multi-head attention, dual-channel GRU, graph convolution, and entropy threshold are unknown. (3) The parcellation and functional integration zones rely entirely on the natural movie-watching task; it remains unclear whether similar patterns of functional integration zones would be observed across other tasks or the resting state. (4) Codes or data are not available, which is important with respect to an atlas paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper offers an interesting perspective by treating model entropy as a biologically meaningful signal rather than something to suppress. 2.The integration zones are supported by multiple independent analyse and explicitly test cross-run reproducibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The description of training is insufficient. “ Training combined cross-entropy loss, cross-session consistency objectives, and mask regularization to promote stable and biologically plausible parcellations. ” What’s the supervised label of cross-entropy loss? How to measure the cross-session consistency? 2.Group priors are mentioned but not specified. The paper states that vertex-level confidence values are “fused with a group-level probabilistic atlas prior derived from a preadolescent Brainnetome atlas,” but the fusion mechanism itself is entirely unspecified. 3.There is no quantitative comparison with existing individualized parcellation methods based on connectivity. As a result, it is difficult to assess whether vertex-wise BOLD dynamics can achieve more stable or reliable parcellations than connectivity-based approaches.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A major strength is the problem formulation. Individualized cortical parcellation remains important, and the use of temporally resolved naturalistic fMRI is a meaningful extension beyond static connectivity-based approaches. The framework is technically coherent, and the probabilistic output is appealing because transitional cortical territories are often poorly captured by hard atlas assignments. The biological framing around SCAN-related integration zones also adds scientific interest beyond a purely technical parcellation study.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not directly compare against strong individualized parcellation baselines, which is a significant limitation for a methods paper. 2.The supervision and optimization targets are not described clearly enough, especially given the difficulty of defining ground-truth labels for individualized areal mapping. 3.The current experiments support entropy as a useful uncertainty proxy, but stronger calibration or external validation would be needed for broader biological claims about integration zones. 4.Alternative explanations such as boundary ambiguity, atlas mismatch, signal quality, or motion effects are not yet fully addressed. 5.The reported reliability evidence appears to rely mainly on within-paradigm splits rather than clearly independent retest sessions, and robustness/statistical reporting remains somewhat limited for a developmentally heterogeneous cohort.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing our core innovations: an uncertainty-aware spatiotemporal graph framework for individualized dynamic cortical parcellations and the validation of SCAN-related integration zones. Below we address the main concerns. R1Q1/R2Q3/R3Q1: Comparison with existing individualized parcellation methods. A: We appreciate this insightful suggestion. Unlike classical approaches relying on static functional connectivity, our key innovation lies in directly modeling dynamic vertex-wise BOLD signals to capture temporal transitions and probabilistic assignments. We agree that systematic comparison with established methods, e.g., Wang et al. (2015), will highlight these dynamic advantages. We will revise the manuscript to better position our method relative to existing individualized parcellation approaches. R1Q2: Ablation of model components. A: Our architecture was designed to address distinct spatiotemporal modeling challenges: local attention captures neighborhood-sensitive BOLD dynamics; the dual-channel design balances each vertex’s own signal with its neighborhood; the GRU models temporal dependencies; and graph convolution respects cortical topology. Together, these components enable the extraction of our entropy-based uncertainty metric. We will strengthen the explanation of how each component supports spatial context modeling, temporal dependency modeling, and topology-aware probabilistic assignment, and present full ablation analysis as future work. R1Q3/R3Q5: Dependence on movie-watching data. A: Naturalistic movie-watching provides rich multisensory stimulation, making it highly suitable for probing integrative cortical processing. We agree that cross-task and external validation will further demonstrate the framework’s broader generalizability. Since no additional task-fMRI paradigms were available in HBN, we are currently conducting experiments using HCP resting-state, task, and movie data. For the present study, we interpret the findings primarily within the naturalistic condition and will discuss its applicability and potential domain shifts in the limitation and future work section. R2Q1/R2Q2/R3Q2: Supervision labels and group prior fusion. A: We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this crucial mechanism. Our model uses the group probabilistic atlas as a soft prior rather than a hard constraint. Specifically, it is concatenated with first-layer GCN features to estimate a vertex-wise confidence map. High-confidence vertices (>0.5) are supervised by atlas-derived pseudo-labels using cross-entropy loss, while ambiguous transition zones are not forced to match hard labels. Cross-session consistency further penalizes inconsistent predictions of the same subject. Thus, the model uses reliable atlas information as weak supervision while preserving probabilistic flexibility for individual integration zones. We will detail these fusion formulations and training hyperparameters in the revised manuscript. R3Q3/R3Q4: Entropy interpretation and alternative explanations. A: We appreciate this insightful comment. A key advantage of STGraph is its ability to quantify parcellation uncertainty from temporal BOLD dynamics. We agree that high entropy requires multifaceted validation to confirm it represents biological integration rather than boundary ambiguity, motion artifacts, or noise. In this study, we evaluated cross-run reliability of candidate integration zones and provided converging evidence from multiple modalities: DTI-based structural connectivity, functional connectivity profiles, meta-analytic decoding, and participation coefficient analysis. We will revise the manuscript to tone down causal claims regarding entropy alone, emphasizing instead that the biological interpretation rests on this multi-modal converging perspective.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important problem in individualized cortical parcellation using naturalistic fMRI. Although reviewers noted limited baseline comparisons, incomplete ablation/training details, and the need for stronger validation of entropy-based interpretation, they agreed that the uncertainty-aware spatiotemporal graph framework is technically coherent and scientifically meaningful. The method is clearly motivated, supported by multiple validation analyses, and demonstrates biological potential.

title: Unveiling Brain-Body Axis Interactions in Psychiatric-Endocrine Disorder with Deep Graph Causal Neural Network
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper proposes a GNN-based causal discovery framework to model directed interactions among 27 white matter tracts, 5 organ systems, and 11 psychiatric/endocrine disorders using UK Biobank data. The authors adopted a masked autoencoder handles missing organ-level features, PCA compresses brain dMRI features, and DAG-GNN learns a directed acyclic graph representing putative causal relationships. They report interpretable brain-body-disease pathways, including convergent white matter vulnerabilities and mediated systemic cascades. The brain-body axis is becoming important more and more for both psychiatric and endocrine diseases. The paper addresses a genuine gap: most prior work examines brain-body links in isolated pairs or uses purely correlational methods. Modeling the full multi-organ, multi-disease interaction network simultaneously is a valuable direction for precision psychiatry and computational medicine. The organ-specific masked autoencoder is a brilient solution to use with UK Biobank analyses. Training on complete cases with synthetic masking, reconstructing only masked entries, and using the learned latent space (rather than imputed values) for downstream analysis is methodologically cleaner than standard mean imputation or deletion approaches. The comparison against Mean+PCA and SoftImpute baselines provides empirical support. The paper carefully ensures that brain (PCA), organ (MAE latent), and disease (embedding) nodes share a consistent feature dimensionality before graph construction. This is a necessary and non-trivial design choice.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Since the entire framework learns from cross-sectional data, argument of causal structure is severely limited. The authors should clearly mention this limitation, and future plan or suggestion for followup study to overcome this. Importantly, due to same reason, the “causal directions” should be carefully re-addressed, otherwise it is well-validated (and known) direction. The discovered DAG is not validated against any external ground truth, alternative causal discovery methods (PC algorithm, GES, FCI, NOTEARS), or known causal relationships from randomized trials or Mendelian randomization studies. Without any form of validation. Although the UKB provides relatively comprehensive data, the sample is not still representative for our species. So, if external validation is not feasible, clearly mention limitation to prevent the over-interpretation of the finding. Minor issues The sample size reduction from 501,000 to 11,628 (due to requiring both imaging and complete organ data) may introduce selection bias that is not discussed. The threshold values for edge filtering (0.5 and 0.2) appear arbitrary; sensitivity analysis would be informative.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1- The author proposed that a directed representation of joint brain–microstructure, organ, and disease relations is an underexplored and clinically meaningful direction, rather than relying on pairwise correlational brain–body studies. 2- The study leverages a large-scale, multimodal dataset such as the UK Biobank, combining diffusion metrics across 27 JHU white matter bundles with organ-level phenotypes spanning musculoskeletal, immune, metabolic, renal, and hepatic systems, along with 11 disease labels derived from ICD-10 and self-report records. 3- Rather than using mean or low-rank imputation, the author used a masked autoencoder for organ-level representation learning to handle missing or zero values. 4- The author shared an anonymized code link (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UKBCausal) for reproducibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1- The paper does not propose a new loss, architecture, or theoretical result. The contribution is largely a pipeline assembly, indicating limited methodological novelty. 2- The author used random thresholds for edges (w > 0.5 for the most essential and w > 0.2 for the second most important) with no sensitivity analysis or justification for these cutoffs. 3- The author did not take into account basic confounders such as age, sex, and head motion. Could you please justify this? 4- Temporal misalignment between brain and organ phenotypes (critical): Section 2.3 explicitly states that brain dMRI features are taken from UK Biobank imaging instance 2.In contrast, Section 2.1 does not specify which instance the organ-level phenotypes (HbA1c, C-reactive protein levels, creatinine, albumin, etc.) come from. Most UK Biobank data for these variables are available only in instances 0 and 1, not the imaging instance. e.g: https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/field.cgi?id=30600 In the UK Biobank dataset, there are four instances: Instance 0: Initial assessment visit Instance 1: First repeat assessment visit Instance 2: Imaging visit Instance 3: First repeat imaging visit 5- The author reports a sample size of 11,628 subjects, but does not provide detailed sample sizes for individual phenotypes after filtering and intersection, making it difficult to assess the effective sample size. 6- The graph is trained and tested on the same dataset (UK Biobank). It would be beneficial to evaluate it on an external cohort as well. 7- All three figures have only one-line titles instead of proper captions. Additionally, in Figure 2 (right), the y-axis is labeled “Number of ROIs (CSV files)”; what does “CSV files” mean in this context?
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: It is an interesting interdisciplinary problem where it integrates brain imaging, organ physiology and disease. It uses large-scale dataset like UK Biobank to provide strong statistical power. The idea of integrating brain + body + disease nodes is novel and it can handle missing organ features y using masked autoencoder. It identifies shared white-matter vulnerability hubs for potential biological insights.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Causal interpretation is weak. The paper claims causal discovery, but data is purely observational cross-sectional. No temporal ordering was mentioned. No mention of potential confouding variables like age, sex. No interventin or instrumental variables were used. DAG-GNN may infer statistical correlation, but interpreting edges as causal mechanism is risky. The authors should clarify assumptions (causual sufficiency, no hidden confouders)and discuss limitations more carefully. 2.Evaluation is weak. The paper mainly evaluates the reconstruction error of MAE, but no quantiative validation of causal structure. It worths doing some prediction evalution or even do some statistical enrichment anlaysis or replication in another dataset. It also lacks comparison with other causal models.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback, which has improved the rigor and clarity of our work. Response to R#1: We agree that the causal interpretation from observational UKB data should be treated with substantial caution. We will tone down strong causal wording and describe the learned DAG as candidate-directed dependencies/hypothesis-generating brain–body–disease pathways, rather than as confirmed biological causality. Since ground-truth brain–body causal graphs are unavailable, longitudinal cohorts, MR, interventional studies, and independent datasets are needed for confirmation. We will also discuss potential UKB selection bias arising from cohort overlap. Response to R#2: We agree that methodological contribution is more accurately framed as an integrated, missingness-aware brain–body–disease framework rather than a new loss, architecture, or theory. Importantly, the integration is not a sequential assembly: MAE, ROI-wise PCA, and DAG-GNN are coupled to build modality-aligned node features for one heterogeneous graph, enabling joint brain–organ–disease structure learning [1,8,23]. Regarding confounders and UKB instances, age, sex, head motion, and temporal differences are important limitations. Organ biomarkers were taken from instance 0, while dMRI features were from imaging instance 2; thus, although organ measures generally precede imaging, edges should not be interpreted as definitive temporal or interventional causal effects. Instead, they represent candidate-directed dependencies requiring further validation. Phenotype-specific sample sizes, filtering steps, and effective sample counts should be reported more transparently, and external-cohort validation remains an important area for future work. Response to R#3: We agree that the causal interpretation from cross-sectional observational data should be handled cautiously. DAG-based structure learning relies on assumptions such as causal sufficiency, the Markov condition, and faithfulness [23], while hidden confounding from age, sex, head motion, medication, lifestyle, and selection effects may remain. Thus, the learned edges should be interpreted as candidate-directed dependencies for hypothesis generation rather than validated causal mechanisms. The MAE reconstruction primarily evaluates the missing-data representation module rather than the causal graph itself; this limitation should be stated more clearly to avoid overclaiming graph validity. Additional prediction tasks, enrichment analysis, external replication, and comparisons with other causal discovery methods would be valuable avenues for future work to validate the inferred structure quantitatively. Response to R#4: We agree with R#4 that several experimental and reproducibility details require clarification. Repeated 5 times means five independent random masking trials for held-out reconstruction evaluation. MAE training used random masking ratios from 10% to 40%, while 30% was used for evaluation as the most common organ-missingness level. The 70% observed-feature threshold was used to balance organ-feature reliability and retained sample size [12]. The mask protocol, disease counts, and organ-specific sample sizes should be stated more explicitly. Our initial bootstrap analysis showed stable recovery of the main pathways, suggesting robustness beyond a single split or threshold. These results were omitted for space because they are supporting rather than central evidence, but can be included in the camera-ready version. Mean+PCA and SoftImpute were included as common linear and low-rank missing-data baselines; their implementation and rationale will be clarified. Minor issues: Figure/caption/ROI issues and the “CSV files” artifact will be corrected in the camera-ready. The thresholds w>0.5 and w>0.2 were used solely to visualize the learned continuous adjacency matrix, and threshold-dependent findings will be interpreted with greater caution in the discussion.

A major concern is that whether it is possible to better validate the derived causal structure. | The reviewers’ concerns were mainly about clarity of methodological and experimental design, which were large resolved in the rebuttal and will likely be resolved in the final version. I believe MICCAI should put more emphasis on multi-modal medical data investigation beyond imaging and single-organ analysis, so I believe the study will potentially become a valuable asset to the community. The paper addresses an interesting brain–body–disease interaction problem using UK Biobank data, and proposes a useful integrated framework combining missingness-aware organ representation learning, imaging feature alignment, and DAG-based graph modeling. The rebuttal appropriately acknowledges that the causal interpretation should be toned down, and that the learned graph should be framed as hypothesis-generating candidate directed dependencies rather than validated causal mechanisms. My acceptance recommendation assumes that the final version will clearly reflect this more cautious framing.
